verses.8: Al-Mizan: On that day, deeds are weighed by truth; those with heavy scales are felicitous.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that those whose scales are light have ruined themselves because they wronged God’s signs.

It says this sūrah shares the principal themes of the chapters beginning with Alif-Lām-Mīm and the chapter beginning with Ṣād; the disjointed letters will be discussed under Chapter 42 (al-Shūrá), by God’s will. Its central subject apparently is God’s covenant with humankind: to serve Him alone and associate nothing with Him. Most nations forgot and broke this covenant; when divine signs and prophets recalled them to it, they denied the signs and persecuted the prophets, apart from a minority.

The covenant concisely contains the whole religious call. People’s receptivity differs, as do the circumstances in which the call reaches them. Some retain their original purity and fiṭrah and therefore believe in God and His signs. Most, however, incline to earthly life and its pleasures, ending in disbelief and defiance. Believers receive divine aid, support, and victory in this world, and are saved from hell for paradise and its blessings in the next. Disbelievers meet God’s wrath, curse, and punishment in this world, which destroys them, ends their progeny, extinguishes their mischief, and leaves them only as ruined stories; the punishment of the hereafter is still more disgraceful, and they will not be helped. This is God’s unchanging custom with former and future peoples: none can repeal His judgment, and He is on a straight path.

For unbelievers, explaining this custom is warning (indhār), calling them to faith in God and His communications. For believers who already know God and His Lordship in general, it is reminder (tadhkīr): instruction concerning God’s signs, names, attributes, and His way of dealing with people in both abodes. Though some verses are disputed, the chapter is Meccan and addresses polytheists and the small body of Meccan believers. Its opening and closing make it a general warning, through proofs, admonitions, and the stories of Adam, Iblīs, Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, Shuʿayb, and Moses; it also reminds believers of God, the hereafter, and His signs.

Al-Mizan notes its discussions of the Hour, the mīzān and aʿrāf; Satan and his hosts; the Qur’an’s taʾwīl; the Throne; tajallī; the covenant in ʿālam al-dharr; al-asmāʾ al-ḥusná; and those mindful of God. It also contains concise legal directives on justice, adornment, and lawful provision. It infers that the chapter preceded Sūrah al-Anʿām: the principle that whatever God has not specifically forbidden is lawful is found here before the more detailed prohibitions of Chapter 6. The relative concision of this chapter’s practical rulings likewise illustrates Islam’s gradual legislation from broad laws to detailed ones.

Concerning (7:1-2), Al-Mizan holds that the indefinite kitābun and the omission of the Sender magnify both the Book and the One who sent it. The consequential fāʾ means that, precisely because this exceptional Book comes from the Prophet’s Lord, he should feel no anxiety in proclaiming it; another book or another sender could warrant such distress because of the difficulty of preaching. Sending the Book has two purposes: warning all people and reminding actual believers in particular. Believers are reminded of their Lord through its signs and teachings, increase in faith, and delight in them; others are warned of divine wrath and punishment in the hereafter and exterminating punishment in this world. The view that “that you may warn thereby” merely completes the command not to be distressed conflicts with the following restriction of reminder to believers. Nor does “believers” include people who were then unbelievers but would later believe: reminder applies to those who are believers in actuality, not merely potentially.

For (7:3), following what the Lord has sent down means adhering to the Qur’an’s correct belief in God and His communications and its righteous practice. The wording indirectly commands acceptance of God’s wilāyah, since the contrast is not with another revelation but with following masters besides Him. The plurality of such masters underscores that God alone is Lord; attentive admonition should make this clear.

For (7:4), the destruction of earlier polytheistic towns manifests God’s consistent custom toward those who took masters besides Him. Bayāt means a nocturnal raid, while qāʾilūn denotes people taking a midday nap. The wording depicts punishment reaching them while they rested securely and heedlessly, whether by night or at midday. Verse (7:5) adds that people inwardly know their wrongdoing in associating others with God. If they will not voluntarily confess it and humble themselves before their Lord, punishment compels the confession; they should therefore acknowledge His Lordship freely rather than by force.

Verse (7:6) follows because people are not free to choose any path without responsibility: they will be questioned about faith and righteous action. Accountability has two sides, the messengers and the people to whom they were sent. The connective marks this as the consequence of the destroyed towns’ confession. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that the first group is prophets and the second angels, because it excludes the polytheists who are the subject of the passage, does not fit the following verse, and has no basis in the preceding context. Verse (7:7) then establishes that God’s questioning rests on flawless, weighty knowledge: without knowledge, people might lie in hope of gain or escape from loss in their terrifying position. God is never absent, has angels record deeds, and Himself encompasses all people.

On (7:8-9), Al-Mizan says that the weighing of the hereafter concerns deeds, not persons as such. It appeals to the scales of justice and reckoning in (21:47) and to the weight of good and evil action in (99:7-8). Deeds annulled through ḥabṭ leave nothing to weigh, as indicated by (18:105); every deed that remains until Judgment is measured. Yet Qur’anic language assigns heaviness to good deeds and lightness to evil ones. It does not portray two piles of good and evil being weighed against each other to determine which predominates; otherwise equality between them would be possible.

There must therefore be an objective external standard by which deeds are heavy or light. As an ordinary measure is determined by its standard unit rather than by the merely preparatory physical apparatus, each act must be matched against its own perfect reality: the true prayer for ṣalāh, or speech free of falsehood for speech. Thus ḥaqq, truth or reality, is the standard of the Day of Resurrection. A deed has weight and value to the degree that truth is present in it; good deeds are heavy because they contain truth, whereas evil is falsehood and vanity and has no true weight. The book of deeds discloses the truth in actions, while the scale determines their weight.

Accordingly, wazn here means weight or heaviness, not the act of weighing. Mawāzīn is the plural of mīzān: every person has multiple scales because every kind of deed has its own measure and its own proper truth. Heavy scales belong to those whose actions contain truth; light scales belong to those who fail to render the right of servitude. Wronging God’s signs means rejecting them, and ruining one’s soul means failing to prepare the provision needed for eternal life and thereby reaching hell. On that day no influence belongs to anything but truth, and all authority belongs to God, the Truth.

Al-Mizan judges al-Kashshāf’s reading—according to which the verse simply says that the true weighing will occur on that day—unlikely except when the verse is detached from its context. It also rejects the majority reading that treats ḥaqq as “just” or “fair” and takes mawāzīn either as the deeds weighed or as multiple scales. Justice in the scales of justice is a quality of God’s just act of setting up and applying the scales, not a quality belonging to the scales themselves; that reading does not explain why good deeds are heavy and sins light. The figurative solution, that heaviness and lightness mean good deeds outweighing evil or vice versa, likewise supplies no criterion by which diverse deeds can be said to outweigh one another. A fair judgment that leaves people no objection requires a real, non-arbitrary basis: the truth present in good deeds and absent from evil ones.

Other exegetes posit a literal worldly-style, two-pan scale. Since they regard actions as vanished aʿrāḍ that cannot return to existence and as lacking physical weight, they variously say that the books of deeds are weighed; that each deed’s manifested effects and signs are weighed; that good and evil deeds appear in fair and foul forms which are weighed; that believers and disbelievers themselves are weighed; or that weighing only manifests each person’s worth, rank, ignobility, or wickedness. Despite their differences, Al-Mizan finds no textual evidence for these accounts and says that all leave the weight of deeds arbitrary, which cannot establish God’s conclusive argument against His servants.

verses.25:
Al-Mizan reads verses (7:10)-25 as an account of how humankind came to be established on earth. In (7:10), tamkīn primarily means making the earth humanity’s dwelling-place, though it can also mean granting power and authority there. The first sense better accords with the later decree that the earth is humanity’s abode and provision for a time. Maʿāyish means the means of living, such as food and drink. Thus the verse recalls two divine favors—settlement or authority on earth, and livelihood—and reproaches humanity’s scant gratitude.

The story beginning at (7:11) elaborates that concise statement. The angelic prostration and Adam’s garden are otherwise distinct accounts, but are joined so that the opening establishment of humanity on earth corresponds to the conclusion commanding descent to earth. Although the address initially concerns all humanity and then names Adam, Adam represents the human race: the prostration was toward humanity, with Adam serving as its qiblah. His khilāfah is not exclusive to him; Satan’s hostility is directed at all humans; and addresses to Adam and Eve elsewhere shift into plural addresses that encompass their descendants. Likewise, Adam’s creation from dust is tantamount to the creation of humanity, whose progeny proceed from him.

The commentary rejects proposed readings that treat thumma in “We created you, then We formed you” as merely “and,” as a sequence only in reporting rather than occurrence, or as referring to formation in loins or wombs without textual evidence. Al-Zajjāj’s explanation—God created and formed Adam and then addressed the angels—is also insufficient if it rests merely on descendants’ blood relation to Adam. For Adam’s acts to be attributed to his descendants, their creation must in some way be incorporated in his; and if his creation represents theirs, the command to prostrate before Adam must likewise concern humanity represented through him.

All the angels prostrated, whereas Iblīs, who was one of the jinn, did not. Though some have proposed that he was included in the command to angels by generalization, or that he received a separate command, Al-Mizan holds that he shared the angels’ station of quds before the command. The command was addressed to everyone occupying that spiritual station. Afterward, the angels remained defined by humble servitude and obedience, while Iblīs exited that station through fisq, whose original sense is a date leaving its sheath. His descent was therefore a departure from divine servitude and proximity, not merely a change of location.

The Qur’anic presentation of command, refusal, argument, expulsion, and reprieve depicts transcendent creational realities in a human social form. Iblīs’ refusal means that he would not humble himself before the reality of humankind, despite his station’s incompatibility with arrogance. The angels’ nature is fixed in obedience and goodness and does not place obedience and disobedience before them as equally available alternatives; Iblīs’ contrary nature is characterized by disobedience. Adam’s creation disclosed this difference, dividing the former common station into proximity and distance, happiness and wretchedness.

Iblīs’ declaration, “I am better than him,” expresses the first disobedience and the root of sins: egoism and self-exaltation before God, to whom all greatness belongs. He regarded himself as independently existent rather than as upheld by his Lord. Had he seen God’s grandeur, he would have been humbled and attended to the divine command rather than comparing fire and clay. His nominal formulation, “I am better than him,” also indicates an established, enduring claim rather than a momentary excuse. God confirms that Iblīs is created from fire, but does not confirm his supposed superiority. Adam’s merit lies not in clay as such, but in his divine spirit, God’s special attention in creating him, and his station of khilāfah. Nothing possesses merit independently; superiority depends on one’s relation to God.

Iblīs’ pride against Adam was therefore consequent upon his deeper pride against God. He overlooked the Commander and judged obedience and disobedience by his own assessment, treating himself as independent and, in effect, parallel to God in greatness. God’s command is true because it is His command and because it corresponds to the realities He creates; it need not be obeyed only after a creature independently recognizes some benefit in it. The Qur’an consequently does not directly answer Iblīs’ comparison of fire and clay, but rebukes his arrogant defiance of God’s command. His argument was qiyās, a probabilistic comparison incapable of establishing truth.

The command to prostrate should not itself be called a takwīnī command, since such a command cannot be disobeyed. Rather, the account portrays the real constitutions and mutual relations of humanity, angels, and Satan through the familiar image of a ruler whose courtiers divide into the obedient and the proud when commanded to honor one specially chosen subject. The prostration represents God’s honoring Adam with proximity, khilāfah, and wilāyah. The angels submit to humanity’s honorable perfection, while Iblīs turns from it because he is inherently opposed to human felicity. Symbolic interpretation is warranted here by evidence, Al-Mizan says, but not indiscriminately: literal meanings remain binding where supported by the Qur’an, sunnah, reason, and the nature of such matters as basic beliefs, law, and the histories of prophets. Symbolic readings may be adopted where evidence excludes literalism, provided they do not oppose an essential belief, a decisive verse, an authentic sunnah, or a proven rational argument.

In (7:13), takabbur is assuming and displaying greatness over another. Any creature’s excellence is from God, so self-exalting pride properly belongs only to God; pride that derives from Him, such as superiority toward God’s enemies, is praiseworthy in that respect, whereas a creature’s independent claim to greatness is blameworthy. Iblīs’ hubūṭ is spiritual relegation from his station of proximity, and his degradation is the fitting consequence of his arrogance. His request for reprieve is granted only until “the day of the known time,” not unconditionally until the Resurrection. This means that his temptations operate until the end of earthly life, not in barzakh, though he may remain with some people after death as an evil companion sharing their punishment.

In (7:16-17), Iblīs claims that, because—or in return for—his being consigned to error, he will ambush humanity on God’s straight path. His sitting in wait means constant ambush upon the immaterial path that leads humans to God and felicity. His approach from the front concerns future hopes, pleasures, ambitions, and fears; from behind concerns children and descendants, whose imagined future may drive people to acquire wealth or make preparations through lawful or unlawful means; from the right concerns religion and the exaggeration or invention of religious practices; and from the left concerns making indecency, sin, and desire attractive. The difference of prepositions used for these directions is, as al-Zamakhsharī reports, a matter of Arabic usage rather than a further difference in meaning.

The grateful in this verse are the same as the chosen servants excluded from Satan’s power elsewhere. The mukhlaṣūn are wholly devoted to God, and the shākirūn have gratitude rooted in them: in every use of anything, they recognize verbally and practically that it belongs to God. Since they see neither themselves nor anything else as independently possessed or controlled, Satan finds no medium through which to tempt them. Their exemption follows from their real condition, not from any favor Satan elects to grant them. Satan transmits perversity through his own perverted condition and affects the human faculty that conceives and confirms what should or should not be done.

God’s threat in (7:18) includes Iblīs and the human beings who follow him. In Adam’s garden, the permission to eat is permissive rather than obligatory, and the prohibition of the tree is advisory: the wrongdoing threatened is self-harm, not violation of an authoritative command. Satan’s waswasah is a quiet prompting toward action; he deceives Adam and his wife by presenting the tree as a way to angelic status or immortality, with the alternate reading also alluding to imperishable sovereignty. A possible interpretation reported by Majmaʿ al-bayān from al-Sayyid al-Murtaḍá—that Satan meant the prohibition applied only to angels and immortals—is rejected in light of (20:120). His emphatic oath that he was their well-wisher intensifies the contrast between professed sincerity and intended deception.

Their tasting of the tree exposes what had been concealed of their shameful parts, and they try to cover themselves with the garden’s leaves. The language of God calling them from afar, and referring to “that tree,” indicates their distance from both their Lord and the tree. Their prayer displays the utmost humility: rather than explicitly demanding anything, they confess their self-wronging, their need for forgiveness and mercy, and the danger of loss. The decree of descent in (7:24) apparently addresses Adam, his wife, and Satan, declaring their mutual enmity and their earthly abode until the end of worldly life. In (7:25), the renewed “He said” likely marks a distinct decree directed especially to Adam, Eve, and their descendants: they are bound to earth in life and death until their resurrection from it.

Al-Mizan criticizes treatments of Iblīs that reduce him to casual curses, human evil inclinations, a merely imaginary story, or sectarian polemic. It rejects claims that Adam was not a prophet, that prophets lack infallibility either absolutely or before prophethood, that all evil and sin are directly God’s acts, or that the story was simply an unexplained test. The fundamental error behind such discussions is failure to distinguish ḥaqīqah, existential reality, from iʿtibār, mental and social convention; and takwīn, creation and causation, from tashrīʿ, legislation.

Three principles clarify the matter. First, existence as such is good; evil is relational, arising where one thing deprives another or conflicts with a proper order. Whatever appears evil must have benefits outweighing its harm, or its creation would oppose divine wisdom. Second, the world is a unified system of diverse, interrelated things. Multiplicity requires difference, including perfection and deficiency, gain and loss, ease and hardship. Without corruption and privation, there would be no health and possession; without misery, no felicity; without disobedience, no obedience; and without punishment, no reward. Obedience is meaningful only where disobedience is possible; otherwise authoritative command, praise and blame, promise and threat, religion, prophethood, social order, and human civilization would lose their meaning.

Satan’s existence as a force calling toward evil is accordingly part of a human world in which perfection is pursued through free choice. He stands, as it were, at the borders of the straight path: a center cannot be defined without sides. The narrative represents a real relation among humanity, angels, and Satan, not an arbitrary celestial drama. It does not follow that the commands and prohibitions within it are takwīnī, for takwīnī commands are unviolable. Adam’s garden was a garden of barzakh, created to manifest human nature before earthly religious obligation. It was neither the eternal paradise from which God’s friends never depart nor an earthly realm governed by authoritative religious commands. Adam entered it as the representative human being, to disclose humanity’s need to live on earth under divine commands and prohibitions; obedience there prepares one for eternal proximity and bliss.

The Qur’an identifies Iblīs as a jinn created from fire, but gives few details about his essence. Its descriptions show that he works through human fear, hope, ambition, planning, lust, anger, and other feelings, influencing thought and decision by making foul acts attractive, offering false promises, and adorning deeds. His sphere is human cognition, and his means are passions and emotions. His temptations are experienced as one’s own ready-present thoughts rather than as an externally heard communication or a conclusion reached by reasoning.

This does not cancel human responsibility. Satan does not compel or replace a person’s knowledge, preference, and will; he only calls, promises falsely, and tempts. Thus, on the Day of Resurrection, he disavows responsibility for those who answered his call. His role and the person’s role have a ṭūlī, vertical causal relation rather than an ʿarḍī, parallel relation: the same voluntary act can be attributed to the human agent and to Satan’s causal influence without making the human act involuntary. Satan’s central deception is to make people view themselves and worldly things as independently existent. This produces heedlessness of God, the root of false belief, illusion, polytheism, and wrongdoing. His influence is pervasive precisely because the person mistakes this induced sense of independence for his own autonomous thought.

The authority of devils over sin resembles the authority of angels over obedience, though God alone is the ultimate authority. Satan has hosts among jinn, humans, and his offspring; the Qur’an does not explain the latter’s procreation. His cavalry and infantry indicate differing speed and strength of operation, while references to devils’ promptings and presence suggest both collective and individual activity. Their acts are attributable to Iblīs as subordinate acts are attributed to a superior. They work in bodily and psychological affairs, in wealth, children, and other worldly concerns, presenting falsehood as truth and evil as good. Their work is ordinarily toward evil and disobedience, though the commentary says one may arguably extend their influence even to some good deeds and acts of obedience. Their action remains imperceptible to humans, showing that they do not operate on the same plane as humans.

A report quoted by Rūḥ al-maʿānī, attributed through al-Shahrastānī to a commentator on the Gospels and also found in the Torah, presents Satan’s objections concerning the purpose of creation, religious obligation, prostration to Adam, his curse, his authority to mislead humanity, and his reprieve. The reported divine reply is that one who truly knew God would know that no objection lies against His acts: “He is not questioned concerning what He does, but they are questioned” (21:23). Al-Mizan holds that these objections can nevertheless be answered by correctly distinguishing divine reality from human conventions and by understanding creation’s order.

God, as the perfect and self-sufficient Origin of all things and source of all goodness, does not act to acquire a perfection lacking in Himself. Creation follows from His essential perfection and origination; its many benefits are not benefits He needs to obtain. In creating humanity, divine wisdom consists in forming from earthly matter a being capable of attaining a degree of proximity unavailable to other creatures. Yet humanity is material, exists among opposing forces, and therefore does not ensure that every individual reaches the species’ ultimate perfection. As with all material species, some members fail under adverse conditions while the species attains its end through those who reach fruition. The perfect human being is the primary end; the failure of some is a secondary and unavoidable consequence of material existence. Disbelief and punishment also culminate in the person’s voluntary choice, even though God’s will encompasses the causal order through which that choice occurs.

Religious obligation does not benefit God, but serves the creature’s gradual movement from potentiality to actual perfection. Although laws and social concepts are iʿtibārī, they link real stages of human transformation. Just as plants require nourishment and animals require the means of their development, humans require divine injunctions to purify themselves and attain the happiness for which they are fitted. Asking why this path rather than another merely raises the same question about any possible intermediary path; moreover, human nature and the laws governing it specifically require religious discipline. Asking why God did not create humans already perfected and eternally blessed asks that material, potential, gradually developing beings be immaterial and fully actual from the outset, which is self-contradictory.

The command to prostrate would have completed Iblīs either in obedience or in disclosed arrogance; he chose wretchedness. It also establishes the human straight path, which requires angels calling to good and Satan and his hosts calling to deviation. Divine curse and punishment are not arbitrary impositions but realities consequent upon arrogant defiance, as death follows poison according to the universal order of causes. Sin necessarily yields punishment unless repentance, intercession, or a good deed brings a forgiveness that overrides it. Satan’s limited authority to call and tempt is likewise required by the contrast in which obedience, truth, and guidance have meaning; he has no coercive authority over God’s servants. A material world without evil, change, loss, potentiality, disobedience, or punishment is not a material world at all.

God is not questioned because He is the ultimate agent and final end: no prior cause supplies His power, and no external good supplies an objective He lacks. Yet this does not license the view that His acts are arbitrary, purposeless, or contrary to reason. Al-Mizan rejects the Ashʿarite conclusion that God may do evil, sin, or purposeless acts merely because human reason cannot judge Him as it judges creatures. It also rejects a Muʿtazilite formulation if it makes human rational judgments precede, delimit, or impose obligations on God. The relevant distinction is between descriptive knowledge of external reality and normative conventions constructed for human action and social welfare. Both ultimately depend upon God’s creation: theoretical reason derives its truths from the created order, and practical reason derives good and evil from the beneficial and harmful consequences built into that order.

Reason therefore cannot stand above God or confine His absolute essence, for its very principles are inferred from His acts. But denying reason’s validity regarding divine action would also destroy the rational basis on which God’s existence and the order of reality are known, reducing all knowledge to sophistry. Human reason can truly affirm divine perfections such as knowledge, power, life, mercy, provision, and guidance, while simultaneously denying from God the limitations inherent in human concepts. It approaches God through tashbīh joined to tanzīh: affirming perfections known by analogy while transcending every finite delimitation.

Likewise, divine legislation has purposes and benefits, but these belong to humanity rather than to God. Divine commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings concern beings who advance from deficiency to perfection by voluntary acts; they cannot be purposeless, just as a path cannot fail to lead toward a destination in the very sense in which it is a path. Good and evil apply to legislation according to whether it guides to benefit or loss, so God does not command indecency, injustice, vain play, or breach of promise. Humans may inquire into the wisdom, benefit, and harm in divine laws, but cannot legislate obligations for God, who needs no perfection and is subject to no authority. His treatment of creatures is nevertheless founded upon proof and just retribution, while His absolute creative and legislative authority remains prior to every standard that human reason derives from His world.
verses.26: Al-Mizan states that God has given Adam’s children garments to cover their shameful parts and adorn them; yet the garment of Godwariness is better and is a divine sign from which they may take admonition.
verses.27: Al-Mizan warns Adam’s children not to let Satan tempt them as he expelled their parents from paradise by stripping their garments and exposing their shameful parts. Satan and his hosts see people unseen, and devils are guardians of those who have no faith.
verses.28: Al-Mizan states that those who commit indecency appeal to their fathers’ practice and falsely claim that Allah enjoined it. Allah does not command indecencies, so this is an assertion about Him without knowledge.
verses.29: Al-Mizan states that God commands justice: people must turn wholly to Him at every place of worship and invoke Him with exclusive faith. As He brought them forth in the beginning, so they will return.
verses.30: Al-Mizan says God guided one group, while error fixed upon another that took devils as guardians instead of Allah and thought itself guided.
verses.31: Al-Mizan commands Adam’s children to wear adornment at every place of worship and to eat and drink without waste, for God does not love the wasteful.
verses.32: Al-Mizan asks who can forbid God’s adornment and good provision for His servants, and states that these blessings will be exclusively for the faithful on the Day of Resurrection. God thus elaborates His communications for people who have knowledge.
verses.33: Al-Mizan states that God forbids outward and inward indecencies, sin, undue aggression, associating partners with Allah without authority from Him, and attributing to Allah what one does not know.
verses.34: Al-Mizan states that every nation has an appointed term which, when it arrives, cannot be delayed or advanced.
verses.35: Al-Mizan states that when messengers from among Adam’s children recount God’s communications, those who are Godwary and righteous will have neither fear nor grief.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan presents verses (7:26)-36 as universal directives derived from Adam’s story. Comparing the accounts in Sūrah al-Baqarah and Sūrah Ṭā-Hā, it holds that commands initially addressed to Adam are here extended to all his descendants. They therefore express laws shared by all religions and show that the principles governing human felicity and wretchedness grow out of Adam’s initial story: the story is the root, and the ensuing laws and order its branches.

On (7:26), Al-Mizan explains libās as clothing that covers the body and rīsh as beauty or adornment, also used for furnishings. God’s “sending down” clothes and adornments apparently means creating them: they come from a hidden source with Him into the visible world according to measure. Though people make garments from cotton, wool, and silk by extracting, spinning, weaving, cutting, and sewing, their existence remains attributable to God, just as all means, powers, and effects ultimately trace to Him. This attribution does not apply in the same primary sense to deficiency, evil, and sin, which are absences of good or violations of God’s command rather than things created as such.

Clothing meets the basic need to conceal parts whose exposure is shameful; adornment is the further desire to beautify oneself. Thus the verse indicates God’s favor in guiding people to make garments and ornaments, and permits clothing for beauty. The better garment, however, is Godwariness. Just as material clothing conceals bodily defects, Godwariness conceals inward defects, including polytheism and every sin. Shame at the exposure of inward defects is more intense and enduring because one faces God’s accounting and the fire that will overspread hearts (104:7). Physical clothing is therefore a sign: reflection on the shame caused by exposed bodily defects should lead one, a fortiori, to recognize the need to cover moral vices and evil habits through the Godwariness commanded and explained by the prophets. Al-Mizan rejects interpretations that identify this garment simply with belief and good works, respectable appearance, ḥayāʾ, ascetic wool, Islam, battle dress, bodily covering, fear of God, or the believers’ clothing in the hereafter, judging them discordant with the verse’s context.

On (7:27), Al-Mizan takes Satan’s stripping Adam and Eve of their garments as a symbol of his action toward all people: through temptation he removes the innate garment of Godwariness given in their fiṭrah. A person remains in the garden of felicity while resisting this deception, but is expelled from it upon yielding to Satan. Satan’s work is especially dangerous because he and his hosts operate unseen and subtly; people may see only themselves acting, not the hidden force directing them toward evil and wretchedness. Devils exercise guardianship by tempting and deceiving those who yield to them, whereas they possess no authority over believers who trust in God, even if believers may at times be tempted. Here lack of faith is not mere passive atheism or polytheism, but deliberate rejection of God’s signs and communications.

On (7:28), Al-Mizan says that the discourse turns to the Prophet and his community. The polytheists defend indecency both by inherited custom and by alleging that God commanded it. The verse directly refutes the latter claim as a false attribution made without knowledge; the appeal to ancestors is likewise defective but lies outside the immediate theme. The exposure and expulsion in Adam’s story itself demonstrate that God is not pleased with indecency. The commentary considers it quite possible that the verse concerns the pre-Islamic custom of naked circumambulation of the Holy House, which some exegetes report was defended as avoiding circumambulation in sinful clothes. Its description as al-faḥshāʾ and its supposed ritual authorization support this application, but the unrestricted wording includes that practice and other similar indecencies.

On (7:29), Al-Mizan contrasts faḥshāʾ, an extreme of vileness, with qisṭ: justice, a fair share, balance, and the middle course between excess and deficiency. Justice in worship requires complete dedication to God, without associating idols or blindly followed ancestors with Him. “Set your faces [toward Him] at every place of worship” means to establish oneself fully for worship, cutting oneself off from every other occupation. Together with invoking God in exclusive faith, it requires that attention be directed to God alone—even worship itself must not become the object of one’s attention, for worship is the act of attending to God.

Al-Mizan rejects readings that make this phrase an instruction to face the qiblah, pray at a particular mosque, attend congregational prayer, or merely obey God alone. The first three do not fit the Meccan situation, when the Kaʿbah was not the qiblah and Muslims did not have numerous mosques; the final reading instead explains the subsequent command of ikhlāṣ.

Al-Mizan links the close of (7:29) to (7:30). It reads farīqan as a ḥāl: humanity will return as two parties just as it was originated as two parties—one guided and one upon whom error is fixed. “The beginning” means the onset of human life, not the whole worldly lifespan. The divine decree that humanity divides thus does not reverse the causal order by which people become misguided: error is fixed upon those who take devils as guardians. The command to justice and exclusive devotion consequently remains meaningful: one should act justly and sincerely in order to be among the guided, not among those led astray through accepting Satan’s authority.

Error becomes especially settled when the erring suppose themselves guided. Those who know they have strayed may return; those who mistake falsehood for truth and evil for good are hardened in deviation. Al-Mizan explains that fiṭrah is inherently directed only to truth, good, and happiness. A person who chooses falsehood, evil, or wretchedness does so because of a mistaken application of this innate orientation: he imagines falsehood true, evil good, and wretchedness felicitous. Thus the innate cognition itself is not changed.

A translator’s note in the passage challenges this connection between (7:29) and (7:30). It argues that the comparison in (7:29) more naturally establishes resurrection from initial creation, while (7:30) is an independent statement in which farīqan is the object of “He has guided,” not a ḥāl describing the return. The note therefore judges Al-Mizan’s comparison of two original and final parties unwarranted and only secondarily related to the verses. Al-Mizan, however, regards alternative explanations—comparison through God’s power, an argument against resurrection-deniers, an entirely unrelated final clause, or resurrection in the state in which one died—as unsupported by the wording or context.

On (7:31), Al-Mizan defines saraf as overstepping limits in any matter, especially expenditure. Wearing adornment at every masjid means dressing well for prayer, circumambulation, and every form of remembrance; its unrestricted form includes Eid prayers, daily congregational prayer, and similar worship. The commands to adorn oneself and to eat and drink indicate permissibility, while the prohibition of waste indicates impermissibility. The address is universal, not confined to a particular religion or group; women are included with men through taghlīb. A translator’s note qualifies that, in the present setting, the primary force of adornment is simply to put on clothing rather than encourage luxury, in contrast to naked circumambulation and the loss of Adam and Eve’s coverings.

Al-Mizan approvingly cites al-Manār’s view that this apparently simple command has reformed societies whose people lacked clothing, advancing their social condition and the manufacture of garments. It also recounts a report that, when Hārūn al-Rashīd’s Christian physician claimed that scripture contained no medicine, ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn b. Wāqid answered that “eat and drink, but do not waste” summarizes it, alongside a Prophetic saying that abstinence is the root of remedy; the physician conceded the point.

On (7:32), the rhetorical question denies that anyone can forbid God’s adornment and good provision. Zīnah removes blame and aversion in social life, and God has brought it forth by guiding human fiṭrah to discover forms of appearance suitable to social relations. It is a fundamental basis of society, since social life cannot dispense with judgments of acceptability, aversion, pleasure, and displeasure. ṭayyibāt are provisions agreeable to human nature, primarily foods but possibly everything needed to sustain life, such as drink, sex, and shelter. The natural faculties and appetites through which people recognize genuine needs provide the clearest evidence of permissibility: God’s takwīn, His creation of human needs and capacities, indicates tashrīʿ, legislative permission.

This permissibility is limited by moderation. Excess and deficiency oppose fiṭrah, harm human faculties and sound reason, threaten social survival, and obstruct a happy life; indulgence in provision or adornment beyond real need pursues a goal contrary to human perfection. The verse’s reference to God’s servants and good provision therefore establishes the lawfulness of natural adornments and provisions, while (7:31) and (7:29) establish the governing limits of non-waste and justice.

Al-Mizan holds that believers and unbelievers share these blessings in the present world, but that the faithful alone will enjoy them on the Day of Resurrection. It rejects an interpretation of khāliṣah as pleasure purified of worldly pain, since the verse gives no indication of pain or limitation, and rejects the claim that believers are the primary worldly beneficiaries while others merely share in their shadow, since the verse establishes no such worldly exclusivity. A translator’s note disputes Al-Mizan’s adopted translation, maintaining that the more apparent reading is that the blessings are for believers in this world and exclusively for them in the hereafter; it also notes Qur’anic contextual evidence for that alternative. Al-Mizan concludes that the elaboration of communications is a special divine favor to people of knowledge.

On (7:33), Al-Mizan completes the account of what is lawful by classifying what God forbids. The forbidden matters divide into wrongful actions and wrongful speech or belief. Actions include fawāḥish, the most vile acts, whether outward or inward; ithm, conduct bringing worldly loss, failure, abasement, and humiliation; and baghy, seeking what one has no right to, including unlawful consumption, oppression, and extortion. The remaining prohibitions are associating partners with God without any authority from Him, and making claims about God without knowledge.

On (7:34), Al-Mizan understands every nation to have a fixed term and lifespan, just as individuals do. In light of Adam’s story, it distinguishes individual persons and societies, addressed by the life, death, and resurrection stated in (7:25), from the whole human species, whose term of earthly abode in (7:24) may end in extinction or the Resurrection.

Finally, Al-Mizan reads (7:35-36) as the last universal address to humankind after Adam’s garden. The intensified condition immā indicates that messengers will certainly come from among people themselves, while yaquṣṣūna means that they explain and unfold God’s āyāt. This is how divine guidance is legislated for humanity: through messengership and revelation. Those who are Godwary and righteous will have no fear or grief; those who deny God’s communications and disdain them will be inmates of the Fire, remaining there forever.
verses.37: Al-Mizan declares that none is more unjust than one who lies about Allah or rejects His signs. Such people receive their decreed worldly portion until the messengers come to take them at death; then, unable to find those they invoked besides Allah, they confess their own faithlessness.
verses.38: Al-Mizan depicts God consigning disbelieving jinn and humans to the Fire. As each nation enters, it curses its counterpart; when all are gathered, the later group blames the former for leading it astray and asks that it receive double punishment. God answers that the punishment is double for each, though they do not know it.
verses.39: Al-Mizan relates that the earlier group will tell the later group that it has no advantage over them, and must taste punishment for what it earned.
verses.40: Al-Mizan states that those who deny and disdain Allah’s signs will not have heaven’s gates opened to them or enter paradise until the impossible occurs: the camel passes through the needle’s eye. This is the requital of the guilty.
verses.41: Al-Mizan says that hell will be the wrongdoers’ resting place, with sheets of fire above them.
verses.42: Al-Mizan says that believers who perform righteous deeds, being tasked only according to their capacity, are the everlasting inhabitants of paradise.
verses.43: Al-Mizan describes paradise as a place where rancor is removed and streams flow beneath its people. They praise Allah for the guidance without which they could not have been guided, affirm that the messengers brought the truth, and are told that they inherit paradise because of their deeds.
verses.44: Al-Mizan recounts the inhabitants of paradise asking the inmates of the Fire whether they too found their Lord’s promise true. After the latter answer yes, a caller announces Allah’s curse upon the wrongdoers.
verses.45: Al-Mizan says they bar Allah’s way, seek to make it crooked, and disbelieve in the hereafter.
verses.46: Al-Mizan describes a veil between the two groups and certain men on the Elevations who recognize each person by his mark. They greet the inhabitants of paradise, who have not yet entered it but eagerly hope to do so.
verses.47: Al-Mizan says, when their look turns toward Fire’s inmates, they pray not to be put among the wrongdoing lot.
verses.48: Al-Mizan says that the occupants of the Elevations will rebuke men recognized by their marks: neither their amassed resources nor their former disdain benefited them.
verses.49: Al-Mizan asks whether these were those denied Allah’s mercy, then commands them to enter paradise without fear or grief.
verses.50: Al-Mizan portrays the inmates of the Fire begging paradise’s inhabitants for water or other divine provision. They are told that Allah has forbidden both to the faithless.
verses.51: Al-Mizan says that those deceived by worldly life, who made their religion diversion and play and denied Allah’s signs, will be forsaken on that Day as they had disregarded its encounter.
verses.52: Al-Mizan states that Allah brought them a Book elaborated with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who have faith.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as the consequence of the universal religion conveyed through God’s messengers. The gravest injustice is either to fabricate a religion and ascribe it to Allah—here especially by associating partners with Him—or to deny His signs, whether the signs of His oneness or the communications that convey His law. Such people nevertheless receive every allotted share of their worldly life: lifespan, provision, health, wealth, and children. The wording that their share reaches them emphasizes that what God has decreed for a person cannot miss him, while what He has not decreed cannot reach him.

At death, the Angel of Death and his assistants ask the polytheists where their alleged partners and intercessors are. Their answer that these have forsaken them means that they no longer find in them the powers of benefit and harm they had imagined. They thereby testify against themselves that they were faithless.

God Himself then commands the disbelievers, jinn and humans alike, predecessors and successors, to enter the Fire. Each entering nation curses the comparable nation before it. The “first” and “last” may mean earlier and later generations, or leaders of error and their followers. The later group asks God to double the leaders’ punishment because the leaders were astray and led others astray. God replies that each has a double punishment: leaders for their own error and for misleading others, followers for their own error and for reinforcing their leaders’ misguidance by following them and swelling their number. Neither group can know the inward pain borne by the other, because each is absorbed in its own punishment. The reply therefore humiliates both groups, after which the former tell the latter that they have no advantage entitling them to a lighter punishment.

The denial and disdain of God’s signs explain this fate. Heaven’s gates are not opened for such people in order that they enter paradise; their admission is made conditional on the impossible passage of a camel through a needle’s eye, and therefore will never occur. Hell is their bed and sheets of fire cover them from above: punishment envelops them from below and above.

By contrast, faith and righteous deeds lead to abiding paradise. Although the plural, comprehensive expression for righteous deeds might suggest an obligation to perform every good act without exception, the qualification that God tasks no soul beyond its capacity removes this burden. Whoever does good to the measure of his ability belongs to the people described.

In paradise God removes ghill, rancor and enmity, whose presence prevents a pleasant life; streams beneath them suggest elevated dwellings. The inhabitants praise Allah, acknowledge that no guidance would have been possible without His guidance, and affirm that the messengers brought the truth. Their ability to render this praise indicates that they have been chosen and purified from false belief and evil action. Their acknowledgment is grateful recognition of the truth of the divine promises conveyed through the prophets.

They are told that this is the paradise they inherit because of their deeds. The distant demonstrative indicates paradise’s exalted significance, not physical remoteness. Inheritance means that paradise was made available to all, believers and disbelievers alike, to be claimed through deeds. The disbelievers forfeit their prospective portion, which believers inherit through their works; without those works they would not inherit it.

The inhabitants of paradise then ask the inmates of the Fire whether they found their Lord’s promise true, and receive their admission. This is a justified rebuke, not vain derision. The believers speak of what “our Lord promised us,” while asking the disbelievers what “your Lord promised.” This may honor the believers as recipients of a promise, but more fundamentally the believers accept resurrection with all the detailed rewards and realities promised to them, whereas the disbelievers confront and deny the general promise of resurrection and requital. The verse does not establish that God must execute every individual threat of punishment merely because He can decline to punish in an individual case. Such a generalization would abolish punishment and render religious injunctions futile. Once both groups have acknowledged the truth of God’s promise, a caller announces to both that Allah’s curse—remoteness from mercy—is upon the wrongdoers.

These wrongdoers bar others from Allah’s way, seek to make it crooked, and deny the hereafter. The description extends beyond adherents of false religions to atheists and materialists. Allah’s way is the path inherent in human fiṭrah and leading to Him. To tread it uprightly is islām, the religion accepted by God; to worship false gods or reject worship altogether is to distort that path and turn God’s blessing into ingratitude. The commentary judges that the caller who proclaims the curse is apparently a human, not a jinn or angel: the Qur’an does not assign jinn a role in the judgment of humans, and, although angels execute divine commands at death and in paradise and hell, the Qur’an explicitly presents humans as speaking, witnessing, and interceding on the plain of resurrection.

The veil between paradise and hell is a real barrier, not a hanging cloth. Al-aʿrāf are its raised crests, from which certain men can oversee both groups and recognize every individual by a distinctive mark. These men are neither angels nor disadvantaged persons whose good and evil are supposedly equal. The indefinite designation “men” magnifies their station and denotes perfected human beings; it can include women by generalization. Angels are not called men, and their merely appearing as men would not justify the designation. Nor do the disadvantaged possess a distinction warranting this emphatic description, and they include women, children, and jinn as well.

The occupants of the Elevations are instead chosen servants of high rank. Their marks disclose not simply whether people are saved or damned, but their particular spiritual traits. They freely address both groups, although only those permitted by the All-Merciful may speak truth on that Day. They greet those destined for paradise, rebuke the proud inhabitants of hell, grant security, and command believers to enter paradise by God’s permission. The account gives no sign that they share the terror of ordinary people on the Day of Resurrection. They thus have the rights, by divine leave, to speak truth, testify, intercede, and command or decree concerning others. This does not compromise God’s exclusive sovereignty: all such intermediary activity is permitted by Him, and the hereafter merely manifests His absolute command without the obscurities that veil it in this world.

The commentary rejects the view that the people of al-aʿrāf are beings held in an intermediate state because their good and evil deeds balance. It records other proposals—that the Elevations are an overhanging place, wall, hill, the wall of another verse, recognition itself, or the Bridge; and that their occupants are angels, people of the fatrah, believers among jinn, children of unbelievers, illegitimate children, the self-conceited, prophets, witnesses, scholars, named members of the Prophet’s family, disadvantaged people, or martyrs who fought without paternal permission. These views reduce broadly to three: exalted human beings, people with equal good and evil, or angels. Though most exegetes favor the second chiefly through narrated interpretations, the commentary holds that the text and context support the first.

A report cited by al-Ālūsī from al-Ḍaḥḥāk through Ibn ʿAbbās identifies ʿAbbās, Ḥamzah, ʿAlī, and Jaʿfar as persons stationed near the Bridge. Tafsīr al-manār rejects it, but the commentary says the report is found in Majmaʿ al-bayān from Tafsīr al-Thaʿlabī, not in a Shiʿa commentary through al-Ḍaḥḥāk as al-Manār claimed. It further maintains that al-Manār wrongly assesses realities of the hereafter by the spatial laws of this world. The existence of one stage or intermediary does not make judgment, reckoning, scales, witnesses, or another stage superfluous. Nor is there any impossibility in the barrier being above the Bridge and al-aʿrāf being its highest part; reports even identify al-aʿrāf with the Bridge.

The greeting, “Peace be to you,” is made by the men on the Elevations to the prospective inhabitants of paradise. The latter have not yet entered paradise but eagerly hope to do so; the subsequent command to enter confirms that this is their condition before entry. The commentary rejects readings that make this clause describe the occupants of the Elevations, whether as an independent statement or as their attribute. Likewise, it concludes that the pronouns in the following prayer—“Our Lord, do not put us among the wrongdoing lot!”—refer to the inhabitants of paradise when their gaze turns toward hell, not to the occupants of the Elevations. The explicit reintroduction of the occupants in the next verse indicates this shift. The phrasing that their gaze is “turned” toward hell conveys the unbearable horror of that sight.

The occupants of the Elevations recognize certain men by more particular marks and rebuke them: their amassed wealth or numbers and their disdain did not help them. They had been proud, contemptuous of truth, and dependent on worldly supports now severed. They then point to the believers whom those wrongdoers had confidently sworn would receive no divine mercy, and command the believers: “Enter paradise! You shall have no fear, nor shall you grieve.” The commentary rejects the suggestion that an unexpressed statement by God or another speaker must be supplied; the context makes this the command of the people of al-aʿrāf.

Thus al-aʿrāf is a lofty human spiritual rank manifested on the Day of Resurrection. Its occupants stand on the crest of the barrier between reward and punishment, survey every person’s unique station and state, speak to whomever they will, give security, and admit people to paradise by divine permission. They transcend the ordinary plane on which people are saved by deeds or damned by sins, while remaining entirely subordinate to the One, All-Paramount God, who may appoint intermediaries to implement His judgments.

The inmates of the Fire then beg the inhabitants of paradise to pour upon them water or some provision given by Allah. Water is singled out because intense heat makes it the foremost request. “Pour” applies broadly to the abundant conferral of blessings, not only to liquids, and the request itself indicates the lofty position of paradise’s inhabitants. They answer that Allah has forbidden both water and provision to the faithless.

The faithless are those who took their religion for diversion and play, were deceived by worldly life, forgot the encounter of their Day, and impugned God’s signs. Diversion distracts from what matters more, play is activity without a real purpose, and worldly deception presents itself as beneficial while intending harm. “Forgetting” here means deliberate disregard: God will therefore forsake them on that Day, withholding what they need for happiness, just as they ignored the Day and failed to prepare for it. Everyone follows some religion in the sense of a path through life. If that path accords with fiṭrah, it leads to true happiness; if people turn from it to merely material and imaginary satisfactions, they make their religion diversion and play.

God has removed their excuse by bringing a Book elaborated with knowledge. “With knowledge” qualifies the bringing of the Book and establishes its truth: its content is revealed according to God’s complete knowledge. Its guidance, in the more fitting sense here, is the showing of the way available to all; its mercy is God’s special mercy for believers. Guidance may also mean bringing one to the goal, in which case it too would belong exclusively to believers.

The Book’s taʾwīl is not merely an interpretation but the external, underlying reality supporting its statements, commands, warnings, and glad tidings. The disbelievers await the manifestation of that reality—the resurrection and requital to which the Book points—despite the proof already completed against them. When it comes, those who formerly disregarded the Book will admit that the messengers brought the truth. Finding themselves devoid of good and ruined by their deeds, they will wish either for multiple intercessors to save them or for a return to the world so that they may act differently. Their fabrications, which had kept them from submitting to truth, will abandon them. The plural “intercessors” indicates that there will be a number of intercessors on the Day of Resurrection.
verses.54: Al-Mizan states that Allah, Lord of all nations, created the heavens and the earth in six days, then settled on the Throne. He covers the day with the swiftly pursuing night, and created the sun, moon, and stars subservient by His command. All creation and command belong to Him, and He is blessed.
verses.55: Al-Mizan: supplicate your Lord secretly and beseechingly; He does not like transgressors.
verses.56: Al-Mizan commands people not to corrupt the earth after its restoration, but to supplicate Allah with fear and hope, for His mercy is close to the virtuous.
verses.57: Al-Mizan states that Allah sends winds as heralds of His mercy. When they carry rain-laden clouds, He drives them to dead land, sends down water, and brings forth every kind of crop. Thus He will raise the dead, perhaps so that people may take admonition.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses establish Allah’s exclusive Lordship. He created the heavens and earth and directs their affairs through an ordered network of causes and effects; He also provides fruits and crops through rain. Since He alone is the Lord and Director of all beings, people must call upon Him and give thanks.

Istiwāʾ means being firmly established or positioned, while ʿarsh literally denotes a king’s elevated seat and, by extension, sovereignty, dominion, and the central point from which affairs are planned and governed. What is known of God’s ʿarsh is only its name: it cannot be a thing carrying God, for God sustains the heavens and earth. In human societies, diverse departments and intermediate authorities are gathered under a single highest authority, the throne. A command descends from that unity through successive levels, taking a form appropriate to each level; conversely, the multitude of particular acts is gathered upward until it reaches that single center.

The commentary holds that this conventional political order reflects an order in creation. Particular events arise through particular causes, which lead back through more universal causes to God. Yet God is not merely a remote cause at the end of a chain: He is present with and encompasses every event and level. Human sovereignty is conventional, whereas God’s mulk is real. The Throne is therefore the single level at which the sovereignty of all diverse causes and effects is gathered, and it is the locus of existential and creational forms directed by God’s command.

Thus, God’s settling on the Throne is a metaphor for His all-encompassing command of His kingdom and direction of every affair in creation. From it proceeds the order by which every being is guided to its end and supplied with what it needs. The succession of night and day, and the subjection of the sun, moon, and stars to His command, expound this direction of affairs. The verse’s image presents night as swiftly pursuing day in order to cover it; it suggests that darkness is the earth’s primary state, while day is an accidental condition arising from sunlight. The celestial bodies follow the course and goal willed for them by God.

Khalq originally signifies taqdīr: giving existence according to measure, determination, design, and arrangement. Amr can mean an affair or condition, and also a command; it is what connects the owner of command with that which is commanded and directs a thing’s movements, actions, and ends. Every thing has an aspect of amr belonging to God. God’s amr is His instantaneous giving of existence: when He wills a thing, His word “Be” bestows existence upon it. Considered in relation to God, this is ījād; considered in relation to the recipient, it is wujūd. God therefore possesses not only the essence of every being but also its qualities, effects, structure, and functioning; nothing possesses anything independently.

Khalq includes all beings, whether composite material beings or simple immaterial ones, and is existentiation according to measure and order. In contrast, amr is existentiation without the aspect of taqdīr. This explains why khalq may be gradual, whereas amr is instantaneous, and why khalq can sometimes be attributed to other beings while amr, in this sense, belongs exclusively to God. Amr functions between God and what He wills to exist, as the spirit functions for the body; phenomena occur by His command.

Khalq and amr are two considerations of one essential reality. When they occur together, khalq especially concerns the giving of existence to a being’s essence, including determination of its features and effects, while amr especially concerns the bringing into existence and management of those effects and the causal order through which beings interact. When used separately, either term may encompass all stages of existence. Accordingly, the verse distinguishes the gradual creation of the essences of heaven and earth from the ordered system by which their affairs are arranged and directed. The conjunction between khalq and amr requires some distinction of consideration, even if not an absolute separation, just as Gabriel may be mentioned distinctly from the angels because of his special rank. Allah is blessed because He possesses abundant good which He bestows upon all whom He sustains as their rabb.

Al-Mizan rejects the view of earlier scholars who forbid inquiry into the deeper realities of such verses and defer their meaning without investigation. This conflicts with reason and with the Qur’an and sunnah, which urge remembrance, reflection, and rational consideration of God and His signs.

It then examines three views of the Throne. The first treats it as a physical couch above the seventh heaven on which God sits. This is the doctrine of the mushabbihah and is rejected as contrary to Qur’an, sunnah, and reason, all of which declare God unlike His creation in essence, attributes, and acts. The second identifies the ʿarsh with the ninth celestial sphere and the kursī with the sphere of fixed stars, assimilating Qur’anic terms to Ptolemaic astronomy. The commentary rejects this identification: its underlying physical principles conflict with Qur’anic and hadith descriptions of veils beyond the Throne, its bearers, the rolling up of heaven, angels who inhabit, traverse, and enter the heavens, heavenly gates, and Paradise at sidrat al-muntahá. Later empirical discoveries also falsified the old astronomical system.

The third view understands the Throne and settling upon it only as a metaphor for dominion or for beginning the direction of affairs. Al-Mizan accepts the metaphorical character of the wording, since no transition, movement, or change can apply to God; temporal verbs attributed to Him describe the coming-to-be of their recipients and the application of His mercy to them. But it rejects reducing the Throne to a merely conventional image. Human authority, rule, and rank are mental and social constructions, whereas when such terms are applied to God they designate real relations in existence befitting Him. Worldly positions and competition for them are diversion and play when pursued apart from an everlasting end; God cannot be subject to such unreality.

The Throne is consequently both a simile for God’s authority and regulation and an external reality: a level of existence at which the reins of all diverse affairs are held. Unlike the illustrative objects in some Qur’anic analogies, the Throne, Tablet, Pen, and Book are indicated by the verses as realities. The Throne is the centralized station through which God governs creation. The statement that He settled on the Throne, directing the command (10:3) explains this meaning.

The same verse’s declaration that there is no intercessor except by His leave concerns creational intercession: the causal means that mediate between God, the ultimate cause, and created effects. Fire, for example, mediates heat, and heat mediates expansion and melting. No cause has efficacy without God’s leave. An intercessor may redirect the course of a prior rule—as the sun mediates light to the earth, or a barrier prevents that light—but both the new course and the means producing it remain within God’s leave and universal direction. Efforts to escape, change, or counter a divine decree through external means or human deliberation themselves belong to that same divine order. Even a thing’s incapacity to receive a higher perfection, or a person’s defiance of a particular divine rule, is acceptance of another rule within the whole system. Opposing causes resemble the two plates of a scale: though moving contrary to each other, both serve one measure.

Thus God alone directs all events, while the Throne is the station of this universal direction. The angels surrounding it carry out His rule and commands; its bearers support the lofty locus from which all divine directions issue. Because the Throne gathers all affairs, it contains their forms or blueprints in an undifferentiated manner and is also a station of divine knowledge encompassing everything. It exists before this visible creation, throughout it, and at the final judgment.

For the command to supplicate, taḍarruʿ means expressing abasement and servility, and khufyah means concealment; the latter may reinforce the former, since one who humbles himself seems to efface himself. These verses conclude from God’s sole creatorship and direction that people must call on Him as servants. Supplication should be humble and not loudly raised, since loudness violates the manners of servitude and is transgression. If the conjunction is taken as alternative rather than cumulative, one may supplicate either beseechingly, normally aloud, or secretly in a low voice. Another possibility is that the terms contrast loud and quiet prayer, with taḍarruʿ replacing mere loudness to show that audible prayer is proper only when it proceeds from humility.

The prohibition of corruption after the earth’s restoration concerns relations among people. Religion requires them to improve their lives by removing injustice and dealing with one another in ways that increase taqwá and bring happiness in this world and the next. Supplication must combine fear and hope. Fear by itself can produce despair and abandonment of worship, while hope alone can produce neglect of the duties of servitude; each restrains the harmful tendency of the other. This balance, together with refraining from corruption, is iḥsān, and Allah’s nearness in mercy to the virtuous is glad tidings for those who answer His call.

The winds are heralds preceding God’s mercy, namely rain, as a herald announces the approach of an awaited traveler. They carry clouds heavy with water, which God drives for, or toward, dead land; He sends down water and brings forth every kind of crop. The revival of the earth proves the possibility of resurrection because like things share the same conditions of possibility and impossibility. Death does not reduce people to absolute nonexistence: though bodies disintegrate, souls remain. This resembles vegetation whose visible parts wither while its roots preserve vegetative life until it becomes active again. The universal revival on the Day of Resurrection is like the earth’s particular revival each year.

Finally, nakadan means sparsely. Read in isolation, the good and bad land may proverbially indicate that good effects issue from good sources and evil effects from evil ones. In the present context, however, the verse means that people receive differing shares of mercy because of differences on their own side; God’s mercy itself is universal and unqualified.
verses.59: Al-Mizan says that God sent Noah to his people, calling them to worship Allah alone and fearing for them the punishment of a tremendous day.
verses.60: Their elite judged Noah to be plainly in error.
verses.61: Al-Mizan says Noah denied being in error and declared himself a messenger from the Lord of all nations.
verses.62: Al-Mizan says Noah conveys his Lord’s messages, is their well-wisher, and knows from Allah what they do not.
verses.63: Al-Mizan says Noah asks why a reminder from their Lord, brought through one of them to warn them, should seem strange, so that they may be Godwary and haply receive His mercy.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan situates Noah’s story after the preceding summons to monotheism and rejection of polytheism and denial of God’s signs. It is the first in a sequence of accounts of earlier prophets. Noah called his people to serve God alone and abandon other gods; most rejected and persistently disobeyed him. The introduction summarizes that God sent a hurricane, saved Noah and those who believed with him, and drowned the rest.

The commentary calls Noah the first messenger whose story is related in detail in the Qur’an, with its fuller treatment deferred to Sūrah Hūd [under verses 11:25-49]. In la-qad, the lām is a vow and an added emphasis suited to polytheists who did not believe in prophethood. Noah’s address, “my people,” manifests his earnest good-will. His command to worship Allah and denial of any other god together establish monotheism: God alone must be worshipped without partners. His fear of punishment on a tremendous day apparently refers to the Day of Resurrection, so the verse contains monotheism and the afterlife. It also arguably implies his messengership, since he brought an unfamiliar form of worship and warned of a punishment unknown to them; his later response shows that they doubted his mission from the outset.

The malaʾ are the community’s chiefs and elite, called so because they fill hearts with awe and eyes with the splendour of adornment and luxury. Their “seeing” is a judgment or opinion. Unable to conceive of someone claiming messengership, warning of punishment, and ordering them to forsake their gods for exclusive devotion to God, they emphatically pronounced Noah’s error manifest.

Noah first negated their charge and then affirmed that he was God’s messenger. By calling God the Lord of all worlds, he affirmed that lordship belongs exclusively to God, against their belief that different gods governed separate realms of creation. His unembellished reply indicates that his freedom from error and his messengership are obvious, unlike their emphatic accusation.

Noah then identifies three connected features of his mission: he communicates his Lord’s many messages, he is their well-wisher, and he knows from Allah what they do not. The plural risālāt indicates messages beyond monotheism and the afterlife. As one of the Resolute Messengers (ūlū al-ʿazm), he had a scripture and a divine code of law (shariah). His good counsel comprises glad tidings that encourage obedience and warnings against arrogant rejection; it rests on God’s teaching about creation’s beginning and end and the divine laws and customs governing the world. What he knows includes the events of the Resurrection, its rewards and punishments, and the outcomes of obedience and disobedience. Some exegetes instead treat the first two statements as Noah’s attributes and the third as a ḥāl qualifying his being their well-wisher.

His question about their finding a reminder brought through a man from among themselves strange is a rebuke for doubting his messengership and the religion of truth. The reminder (dhikr) is that by which God is remembered, namely the divine teachings revealed to him; “from your Lord” implies a reminder which is from Him. It came so that the messenger might warn them, they might become Godwary, and God’s mercy might haply embrace them. Although taqwá leads to salvation, it is not its complete cause, which accounts for laʿalla and its tentative force. The verse thus briefly summarizes Noah’s divine teaching.

When they denied him, God delivered Noah and those with him in the ark (al-fulk) and drowned those who denied His signs. Fulk means a ship or vessel and may be singular or plural. Their being a blind lot (ʿamīn) means blindness of insight, rather than the blindness of sight denoted by aʿmá.
verses.65: Al-Mizan relates that Hūd, brother of ʿĀd, calls his people to worship Allah alone and be wary of Him.
verses.66: Al-Mizan reports that the faithless elite of Hūd’s people call him foolish and a liar.
verses.67: Al-Mizan reports that Hūd denies folly and affirms that he is a messenger from the Lord of all nations.
verses.68: Al-Mizan reports that Hūd conveys his Lord’s messages as a trustworthy well-wisher.
verses.69: Al-Mizan relates Hūd’s rebuke at their surprise over a human warner. He reminds them that Allah made them successors after Noah and increased them in creation, calling them to remember His bounties so that they may be felicitous.
verses.70: Al-Mizan reports that they reject worship of Allah alone for their ancestral worship and mockingly demand the punishment with which Hūd threatens them.
verses.71: Al-Mizan reports Hūd’s declaration that punishment and wrath are due against them, his rejection of their inherited and unauthorized divine names, and his warning that they and he must await the outcome.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains that calling Hūd the “brother” of ʿĀd uses akhū metaphorically for his relation to his people, not necessarily biological kinship. It reports al-Zamakhsharī’s view that, unlike Noah’s account, the absence of a conjunction before “He said” answers the expected question of what Hūd told ʿĀd; the preceding story has already established the pattern of a messenger addressing his people.

The qualification that the elite were faithless, according to al-Zamakhsharī, indicates that some elite believers concealed their faith, unlike Noah’s people. The emphatic accusation of safāhah reflects their shock at a challenge to entrenched idolatry; they called Hūd unintelligent and, apparently, counted him among the prophets they regarded as liars. Although ʿĀd were more insolent than Noah’s people, accusing Hūd of folly rather than merely erroneous judgment, Hūd courteously calls them “my people,” showing compassion and a desire to save them. He simply denies the charge and affirms his evident messengership.

As a messenger, Hūd’s task is only to convey his Lord’s messages. His description of himself as amīn answers their charge of lying: he has not violated their rights. As nāṣiḥ, he is free of falsehood, does not deceive in his preaching, and has not betrayed the true message; he calls them to monotheism because it is true and benefits them.

Hūd reproves their wonder that a warning should come through a man among themselves, then recalls Allah’s blessings. He made them successors after Noah and especially increased their physical creation, giving them strength and capability; this indicates that ʿĀd preceded later post-Noah civilizations and possessed great might. Baṣṭah means expansion or increase, and ālāʾ means bounties. Their reply displays adherence to their forefathers’ worship and mockingly challenges Hūd to bring the threatened punishment.

Rijs and rijz can denote something from which one is removed or shunned, hence filth and punishment. Because ʿĀd persisted in inherited idolatry, Hūd declares that Allah’s punishment and wrath—separating them from Him—have become due. His command to wait indirectly but certainly threatens the punishment they demanded.

Their argument for their gods rests on finding their supposedly more perfect forefathers worshipping them and therefore following them. Hūd answers that neither they nor their fathers possess sulṭān, a decisive proof, for their gods’ divinity. Their gods are thus only imagined labels—such as gods of fertility, war, sea, or land—rather than realities. The commentary holds that any claim unsupported by rational proof is a mere appellation, and relying on appellations is ignorance. The same applies wherever people treat something other than God as independent, obey it, or seek its favor: the Qur’an counts such obedience and reliance as ʿibadah (worship, service).

The indefinite “mercy” signifies Allah’s special mercy for believers, by which He helps them according to His promise. Cutting off the dābir of those who denied His signs means annihilating them and uprooting their lineage: dābir denotes what is behind something, including a group’s remnant or a person’s succeeding generation. Al-Mizan defers a fuller discussion of Hūd’s story to Sūrah Hūd [under verses 11:50-60], by God’s will.
verses.73: Al-Mizan recounts that Ṣāliḥ called Thamūd to worship Allah alone, presenting Allah’s she-camel as a manifest sign. They were to let it graze freely in Allah’s land and not harm it, lest a painful punishment seize them.
verses.74: Al-Mizan states that Allah made Thamūd successors after ʿĀd and settled them in a land where they built palaces on its plains and carved homes from mountains. Ṣāliḥ therefore calls them to remember Allah’s bounties and refrain from corrupting the earth.
