verses.75: Al-Mizan relates that the arrogant elite asked the abased believers whether they knew Ṣāliḥ had been sent by his Lord; the believers affirmed faith in his message.
verses.76: The arrogant declared their disbelief in what the believers believed.
verses.77: Al-Mizan says they hamstrung the She-camel, defied their Lord’s command, and dared Ṣāliḥ, if a messenger, to bring his threatened punishment.
verses.78: An earthquake seized them, leaving them lifeless and prostrate in their homes.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan explains that Ṣāliḥ, who was of Thamūd’s own tribe, called his polytheistic people to worship Allah alone, as Noah and Hūd had called their peoples. The commentary initially describes Thamūd as ancient Arabs living in al-Aḥqāf in Yemen, but a translator’s note identifies this as a mistake: ʿĀd lived in al-Aḥqāf, as stated in verse 46:21, while Thamūd lived in al-Ḥijr, mentioned in verse 15:80.

The bayyinah is a decisive witness or evidence: the she-camel, which God brought forth from the mountain in response to Ṣāliḥ’s supplication. Calling it Allah’s she-camel denotes its special divine relation and attention (ʿināyah). The command to let it graze follows from its being a divine sign. It was a burdensome restriction whose violation could bring the exterminating punishment that finally decides between a prophet and his people; the commentary cites, “There is a messenger for every nation; so when their messenger comes, judgement is made between them with justice, and they are not wronged (10:47).” Referring to the land as Allah’s land alludes to the difficulty of this requirement; a translator’s note explains that they had no right to prevent His she-camel from grazing in His land. Ṣāliḥ warned them not to impede, hamstring, or slaughter it, lest painful punishment befall them.

Ṣāliḥ also reminded them that Allah made them successors after communities such as ʿĀd and established them in the land, enabling them to build fortified dwellings on its plains and carve houses in its mountains. Bawwaʾa means to establish or give a dwelling; suhūl are lowlands, opposed to mountains. The subsequent command to remember Allah’s bounties concludes this enumeration: after their blessings have been set out for them, they must remember them. The prohibition on acting wickedly and causing corruption necessarily follows from that remembrance. For ʿathy, the commentary reports the meanings corruption, disturbance, and excess; al-Rāghib distinguishes ʿayth, more often used for sensibly perceived corruption, from ʿathy, more often used for intellectually perceived corruption.

The phrase “those among them who had faith” interpretively restates “those who were abased”: the mustaḍʿafūn were the believers, and the believers were the mustaḍʿafūn. None of the arrogant elite believed in Ṣāliḥ. When they later hamstrung the She-camel, ʿaqara may mean slaughtering it or cutting its legs. Their ʿutuww was revolt and refusal, and its construction indicates that this defiance of their Lord’s command arose from arrogance and pride.

Al-rajfah means severe shaking or vibration. The verse attributes their death to such a quake, while elsewhere the punishment is called the Cry (11:67) and a bolt of humiliating punishment (41:17). The commentary connects these descriptions by saying that thunderbolts bring terrifying roars and their atmospheric turbulence usually reaches the earth as a quake; it is also possible that rajfah means the quivering of their hearts and bodies from terror. Thus their punishment was a heavenly bolt accompanied by a dreadful cry and a quake in the earth or their hearts. They were left jāthimīn—fallen on their faces and knees—in their city, called their homes. Yet the verse’s concern is not the mechanism of the exterminating punishment, but that it was directed against them for disbelieving in and wronging Allah’s sign and miracle. Ṣāliḥ then abandoned them to their fate, declaring that he had conveyed his Lord’s message and sincerely wished them well, but they did not like well-wishers.
verses.80: Al-Mizan states: Lot rebukes his people for committing an unprecedented outrage.
verses.81: Lot charges his people with desiring men rather than women and calls them profligate.
verses.82: Al-Mizan states: His people’s only reply was to demand that Lot and his followers be expelled as puritanical.
verses.83: Al-Mizan states: God delivered Lot and his family, except his wife, who remained behind.
verses.84:
Al-Mizan says that the opening “and” apparently either links Lot’s story to the series beginning with Noah—meaning that God sent Lot—or, as is usual in such Qur’anic openings, implies the omitted command udhkur, “remember”: remember Lot, whom God sent. Lot’s introduction differs from that of Hūd and Ṣāliḥ apparently because he followed Abraham’s code of law, whereas they followed Noah’s religion; the subsequent return to the earlier form for Shuʿayb likewise reflects his following Noah’s code. Lot was sent to Sodom and its vicinity to call its polytheist, idol-worshiping people to monotheism.

The commentary identifies al-fāḥishah, “indecency, outrage, flagrant act,” as lawāṭ (sodomy, homosexuality), as the following verse clarifies. “None of al-ʿālamīn” means no human communities or nations, showing that the history of homosexuality goes back to Lot and his people. “Coming” (ityān), qualified by lust and by its being instead of women, indirectly denotes intercourse; they had abandoned mating with women and satisfied desire only with men. They are musrif because they exceeded the limits of their natural makeup. Inna indicates the certain realization of the act, while an implied interrogative hamzah makes the statement a shocked rhetorical question, emphasizing the unbelievable indecency they had invented.

Lot’s people had no answer to his challenge: they should either have shown his judgment mistaken or admitted it, but instead threatened expatriation. Their irrelevant reply displays both their lack of an answer and their lack of intelligence. Their demand to expel Lot and his followers is contemptuous: it treats the town as belonging to its people, Lot’s party as foreign immigrants who keep themselves pure from the people’s practices, and them as few and weak. The deliverance of Lot’s household shows that none outside his family believed, as also indicated by: but We did not find there other than one house of muslims [or submitters] (51:36). His wife’s being among al-ghābirīn, those left behind, indirectly means that she was killed.

Al-Mizan observes that the context calls for the people’s exterminating punishment, so the rain was their punishment. Its indefinite form (nakirah) indicates an unusual event of tremendous impact, explained elsewhere: and We rained on it stones of laminar shale, marked with your Lord [for the profligate], never far from the wrongdoers (11:82-83). The command to observe the guilty people’s fate addresses the Prophet Muḥammad so that he and his nation may take a lesson.
verses.85: Al-Mizan relates that Shuʿayb called Midian to worship Allah alone, citing a manifest proof from their Lord. He commanded full measure and balance, forbade cheating people of their goods and corruption after the earth’s restoration, and said this is better for them if they believe.
verses.86: Al-Mizan relates Shuʿayb’s prohibition against lying in wait on roads to threaten believers, bar them from Allah’s way, and seek to make it crooked. He urges his people to remember how Allah multiplied them from few and to consider the fate of corrupters.
verses.87: Al-Mizan says believers and unbelievers should be patient until Allah, the best of judges, judges between them.
verses.88: Al-Mizan relates that the arrogant elite threatened to expel Shuʿayb and his faithful followers unless they returned to the people’s creed. Shuʿayb rejects this even if they are unwilling.
verses.89: Al-Mizan relates Shuʿayb’s declaration that returning to their creed after Allah delivered them from it would fabricate a lie against Allah. They cannot return unless Allah, their all-knowing Lord, wills it; they trust Him and ask Him to decide justly between them and their people as the best of deciders.
verses.90: Al-Mizan states: The faithless elite warn that whoever follows Shuʿayb will be a loser.
verses.91: An earthquake seized them, leaving them lifeless and prostrate in their homes.
verses.92: Al-Mizan says that those who impugned Shuʿayb became as though they had never lived there; they were the true losers.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan explains that Shuʿayb’s story continues the series beginning with Noah and, like the preceding prophetic missions, rests on monotheism. His “manifest proof” establishes that he had a miracle proving his messengership, though the Qur’an does not identify it. The exterminating punishment of his deniers cannot itself have been that proof, since it killed those who needed the proof; the fāʾ introducing the ensuing commands indicates that they followed the miracle and were issued before the punishment.

After commanding worship of Allah alone, Shuʿayb orders fair measure and balance and forbids depriving people of their goods, indicating prevalent financial corruption and unjust dealing. He also forbids corruption after the earth’s restoration. Allah has set the earth right both through its natural creation and through human fiṭrah, which moves people to preserve social order and prosperity. Although the unqualified term includes every sin against Allah or people, its context more particularly concerns corruption that destroys social security in lives, dignity, and property, such as robbery, slander, unjust killing, and banditry.

The statement that this is better concerns the commands about fair dealing and social corruption, not the preceding command to worship Allah. Society depends on secure exchange: people trade what they possess in excess for what they need, and this requires confidence in the quantity and quality of goods. When a person permits himself to cheat, he in effect permits its universal spread; widespread fraud leaves no assurance that remedies are not poison, good goods not inferior, or genuine products not adulterated, with grave human and financial costs. Likewise, without safety and security, social activity and production stop, resulting in the loss of crops, people, and humanity.

The commentary takes īmān here in its literal sense of trusting, accepting, and confirming Shuʿayb’s word: either people who confirm it will gain the benefits of these commands, or those who trust the truth will recognize that the commands serve their own interest. Some exegetes instead take īmān technically: one view says unbelievers gain no real benefit because disbelief brings eternal wretchedness and worldly gains are fleeting; another makes dhālikum refer to everything previously mentioned. The latter makes the statement virtually tautological, since worshipping Allah entails belief in Him. Both technical readings also conflict with the apparent force of kuntum muʾminīn: its past-tense verb and active participle indicate an established quality, not an invitation to a mixed community to acquire religious faith. Had that technical meaning been intended, the verse would apparently have said “if you believe.”

For (7:86), the commentary reads “threatening and barring” as circumstances qualifying those who lie in wait, and “seeking” as qualifying their barring. This is Shuʿayb’s third specific command: his people must not obstruct the straight path, Allah’s religion, by stopping, threatening, and deterring believers from faith, meeting and listening to Shuʿayb, and practising religion with him. Polytheists sought to make Allah’s way crooked—the way of fiṭrah—and employed every means to cut off faith. Shuʿayb therefore reminds them of Allah’s favors and of the fate of corrupters.

Their multiplication after being few is among Allah’s greatest blessings. Human beings need society to fulfil their many needs; through cooperation in thought, decision, and action, growing numbers enlarge collective knowledge, choice, and power, enable discovery of subtler needs, and provide more advanced means of mastering natural forces. A populous nation thus surpasses a small group vulnerable to enemies and dependent on others in government, economy, and military affairs. Conversely, historical tyrants who devastated towns, shed blood, enslaved people, and grew arrogant in worldly power were eventually stripped of their influence and bounties after abandoning reason for desire and worldly diversion. This illustrates a divine custom: human life endures through reason, whereas corruption that transgresses its bounds, individually or collectively, is opposed and crushed by the forces of creation.

Verse (7:87) is Shuʿayb’s fourth specific command. Foreseeing an unavoidable division between believers and unbelievers, and apparently anticipating that the arrogant elite would persecute believers and weaken their resolve, he orders patience until Allah judges. This serves both groups: believers can live peacefully without uncertainty in their religion, while unbelievers avoid impulsive and ignorant injustice. Allah judges at the proper time and wrongs no one. Thus the command is advisory (al-amr al-irshādī) for unbelievers, who did not accept Shuʿayb’s religious and legislative authority, and also authoritative (al-amr al-mawlawī) for believers.

The arrogant elite reject this counsel and emphatically threaten to expel Shuʿayb and the believers unless they return to polytheism. The stressed forms of “we will surely expel you” and “you shall surely revert” show their firm resolve. Shuʿayb speaks for himself and the believers in answering, “Even if we should be unwilling?!”: if forced to choose between expulsion and reversion, they will not choose reversion.

In (7:89), he explains that returning to their creed would falsely ascribe partners, as well as false laws and claims, to Allah. The commentary rejects the inference that “after Allah has delivered us from it” means Shuʿayb had once been an idolater. He speaks for the whole body of believers, most of whom had been polytheists before Allah guided them through him; a group may be described by what applies to most of its members. Alternatively, deliverance may be real deliverance from every actual and hypothetical error. On this reading it applies both to Shuʿayb, who never associated anything with Allah, and to his formerly polytheist followers, since every soul left to itself is on the way to perdition and every good comes from Allah.

“It does not behoove us to return” advances from mere unwillingness to an absolute refusal. Yet Shuʿayb adds “unless Allah, our Lord, should will so” out of prophetic courtesy toward Allah’s unrestricted authority. A human being may err, and Allah may withhold His special attention and remove faith as punishment; therefore anyone may fall into error and perish. By saying “Allah, our Lord,” Shuʿayb distinguishes monotheism from the idolaters’ belief in Allah as highest deity alongside multiple lords governing separate domains: Allah alone is both deity and Lord, ruling and directing all affairs. “Our Lord embraces all things in [His] knowledge” explains the exception, since Shuʿayb knows only what Allah teaches and Allah may will what he does not know. Their trust in Allah is reliance on the One who suffices and protects against feared evil.

Shuʿayb’s prayer for Allah to “decide” justly asks for fatḥ—an opening or separation—between the believers and the polytheists, a decisive final judgment that separates the two and entails the destruction of wrongdoers or something comparable. He does not specify who will be saved, destroyed, victorious, or defeated, but defers the matter justly to Allah. This displays the same courtesy as his earlier call to await Allah’s judgment. Khayr al-Ḥākimīn and Khayr al-Fātiḥīn are excellent names of Allah.

The elite’s warning in (7:90) may mean that following Shuʿayb is believing in him; it is then another instance of their threatening and barring believers and prepares for the later reversal that his impugners are the losers. It may also mean physically following him. Having offered Shuʿayb and his companions expulsion or return to their creed, they understood from his refusal and prayer that he would migrate and his believers would follow. They therefore used fearmongering to keep the believers behind so that Shuʿayb would leave alone; he was their primary enemy.

In (7:91), aṣbaḥa means “became” or “turned out,” though it can also mean entering the morning. The earthquake seized the deniers and left them dead in their homes. Al-Rāghib, as cited in the commentary, says that ghaniya with fī and a place means dwelling there for so long as to be sufficient of any other abode. Thus (7:92) compares those who rejected Shuʿayb to people who seem never to have settled there. Though they had been rooted in their land for generations, with homes, kinship, property, and investment that normally make departure nearly impossible, they lost everything instantly when the earthquake struck and died where they lived.

Their expectation that Shuʿayb and his followers would lose recoiled upon them. The Qur’an first reports their claim, then mentions that “the earthquake seized them” without initially naming its victims, and finally identifies “those who impugned Shuʿayb.” This sequence makes clear that Allah’s judgment favored Shuʿayb and his followers and that the rejecters were the losers caught in a plot. Finally, Shuʿayb’s turning away after their punishment and death, declaring that he had delivered his Lord’s messages and sincerely wished them well, is a lesson for others. His question, “How should I grieve,” uses āsá, derived from asá, meaning grief or sorrow, and denies grief for a faithless people.
verses.94: Al-Mizan says that God sent no prophet to a town without afflicting its people with misery and hardship so that they might entreat His forgiveness.
verses.95: Al-Mizan says God exchanged evil for good until they multiplied; after dismissing hardship and ease as ancestral, they were seized unawares.
verses.96: Al-Mizan states that faith and Godwariness would have brought a town blessings from heaven and earth, but its denial led God to seize it for what it had earned.
verses.97: Al-Mizan asks whether townspeople can feel safe from God’s punishment coming upon them at night as they sleep.
verses.98: Al-Mizan asks whether townspeople can feel safe from God’s punishment coming upon them at midday while they play.
verses.99: Al-Mizan declares that only losers feel secure from Allah’s devising.
verses.100: Al-Mizan asks whether those who inherit the earth after former peoples have not been shown that God may punish them for their sins and seal their hearts, leaving them unable to hear.
verses.101: Al-Mizan says that the towns’ messengers brought manifest proofs, yet their people could not believe in what they had previously denied; thus Allah seals the hearts of the faithless.
verses.102:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses conclude the accounts of earlier nations: most violated the covenant of servitude and therefore encountered a recurrent divine order. When God sends a prophet, He afflicts the people with misery and hardship so that they may humbly return to their Lord. When they turn away from these signs instead, their hearts are hardened and sealed, they are diverted from truth and attached to bodily pleasures and material luxury; this is makr, divine devising. Then comes istidrāj, gradual ruin through blessings: hardship becomes ease and punishment bounty, leading them little by little to a sudden punishment when they least expect it. Their security, complacency in their knowledge, and confidence that their devices can ward off threats leave them unprepared.

The commentary takes faith and Godwariness as the stated criterion for earthly blessing. Existence is one interconnected whole, whose parts move toward God and toward their appointed perfection. When a central part, especially a human society, departs from its proper path, it harms the related parts of the whole; that disruption returns upon it as affliction. If it realigns itself, it recovers its sound condition. If it persists until its corruption threatens surrounding beings, the other parts of existence resist it through the force God has placed in them, and destroy it unexpectedly.

No human society is exempt. A nation that departs from its fiṭrah (primal nature, innate disposition, initial makeup) and from the perfection set for human life disturbs the connected causes and forces of existence. This rebounds as social and moral decay, hard-heartedness, loss of compassion, epidemics, and natural disasters: the sky may withhold rain, the earth crops, and destructive events may multiply. Such afflictions are signs intended to awaken people to repent and return to the straight path of their fiṭrah; both hardship and ease are trials. If they return, the purpose has been achieved, though this has rarely occurred. If they persist, they become accustomed to a life of friction with the world and seek safety in scientific and technological means against calamities.

Al-Mizan rejects the thought that scientific advancement can make humanity master nature or overturn the laws of existence. Human beings are themselves a small part of that system, and their plans and mechanisms rest on its general laws. It also rejects the claim that religion denies natural causality and merely assigns unexplained events to a competing supernatural cause. God is not a cause parallel to physical causes: He encompasses all things, creates every cause, guides each cause to its effect, and controls its creation, function, and effect. Human volition, thought, and technology belong to the connected causal order through which God implements His decree. Thus people cannot oppose God in His kingdom by the very means He has created.

God has created and measured all things, guided each toward its perfection, and made nothing futile. Every being has a path to its bliss through fiṭrah. One that follows this divinely intuitive path reaches its end; one whose deviation cannot be returned to the straight path loses its intended goal and becomes subject to punishment. Accordingly, when humanity lives harmoniously with existence, the world is harmonious to it and heaven showers blessings; when humanity corrupts itself, existence reciprocates that corruption. Repentance restores the proper order, but entrenched corruption brings the destruction of its foundations.

On verse (7:94), Al-Mizan notes differing lexical opinions over whether baʾsāʾ and ḍarrāʾ concern bodily or financial misfortune. From the following contrast of ḍarrāʾ with sarrāʾ, however, it infers that ḍarrāʾ means every unhappy event in an unrestricted sense, while baʾsāʾ is a particular instance of misfortune. The verse states a divine custom: God afflicts the bodies and possessions of a people to whom He sends a prophet so that hardship may make them entreat and seek refuge in Him, thereby assisting the prophet’s call to faith and righteous works. Blessings commonly distract people and make them feel self-sufficient, whereas their loss awakens fiṭrah to the need for the One able to remove deprivation and disgrace. Prophetic instruction may then guide those who had not recognized this truth.

On verse (7:95), evil and good respectively mean distress and comfort, fear and hope, or hardship and ease. Although ʿafw may mean abundance—an increase in people and wealth after affliction—Al-Mizan considers it also likely to mean the effacement of traces: the newly given good erased the signs of their former evil condition. The people consequently treated alternating hardship and ease as ordinary fluctuations of nature, also experienced by their fathers, rather than divine trials. They forgot their misery when blessings came, though they should instead have become mindful and more grateful after their earlier entreaty. They replaced the end God intended for them with another end, and their hearts were sealed so that they could no longer hear truth. Their sudden seizure exposes their ignorance of how God governs the world: confident in their knowledge and defensive devices, they suppose themselves able to protect themselves from destructive forces.

On verse (7:96), barakāt means abundant good of every kind, including security, comfort, health, wealth, and children. Blessings are portrayed as channels which God opens: heavenly blessings include rain, snow, heat, and cold in their proper beneficial measure, and earthly blessings include grain, fruit, and security. The verse concerns a people collectively: it is not enough that only some possess īmān (belief, faith) and taqwá (Godwariness, self-restraint), since the disbelief and sin of others produce decay and corruption. God’s seizing is seizure for retribution; its reality is that people are given back the consequences of what they have earned.

Verse (7:97) follows from this warning. Bayāt and tabyīt denote attacking an enemy at night, and night is a time of rest in which people are naturally cut off from what is outside them. Since sensory enjoyments veil townspeople from realities beyond them and punishment may overtake them unawares, they cannot feel immune from its arrival during sleep. In verse (7:98), ḍuḥá is the forenoon, when sunlight has fully spread. “Playing” refers to pursuits of worldly aims and material pleasures when they are not directed toward truth and eternal happiness; such occupations are mere sport and play. It may also be an indirect reference to heedlessness, just as sleep may indirectly refer to heedlessness in the preceding verse.

Makr in verse (7:99) is directing harm, or what leads to harm, toward someone without that person’s awareness. As a divine act, it is always retributive: after disobedience, God may seize someone unexpectedly or treat him in a way that leads him toward punishment without his knowing. God does not exercise makr against a servant without a preceding violation. The three questions of verses (7:97)–99 are rebuking rhetorical questions. The repeated noun in the question about midday means that the punishments of night and day are independent, so either may strike a people. The pronoun in verse (7:99) gathers both groups, making the verse their conclusion. Feeling secure from God’s makr is itself part of that makr, for this very false immunity leads to punishment; those who feel secure are therefore losers.

On verse (7:100), those who inherit the earth are the later generations who receive it after their fathers. The stories already recounted are what “guide” them, in the sense of clarifying for them, that God may punish them for their own sins and seal their hearts. The point is that nothing can obstruct God or protect these inheritors from His might. The sealing clause is joined to the statement of punishment and means that, if God wills, He may also seal their hearts so that they do not hear.

Verse (7:101) gives a second summary of the earlier stories. The first summary viewed God’s treatment of the peoples through affliction, ease, and sudden seizure; this one views their response to the religious call. Although messengers brought manifest proofs, the peoples lacked the readiness to accept what they had formerly denied, and this inability resulted from the seal on their hearts. The phrase “in what they had disbelieved earlier” means the very object earlier rejected, not merely disbelief as a cause; the parallel wording with bihi confirms this. “They were not to believe” signifies that they were not in a state prepared to believe.

Al-Mizan presents compatible levels of the earlier denial. First, people denied the divine signs implicit in hardship, which should have moved them to entreat God, and in later ease, which should have moved them to gratitude. Calling both conditions mere natural fluctuation rooted that denial in their hearts; thus, when the prophets later called them to the same truth, they could not accept it. Second, they had already rejected the guidance of their own intellects, which tells them that they are under God’s authority and should serve Him alone; they therefore rejected the same reminders when the prophets brought them. Third, this intuitive covenant also existed in the prior realm when God made Adam representative of humankind, ordered his descent to earth, and covenanted with him and his descendants to worship God without associating partners. In that prior realm, divine taqdīr (measurement, ordainment, predestination) guided one group while another deviated; in this world, error became fixed on the latter after their evil deeds. This inner level does not contradict free human choice in attaining felicity or wretchedness, nor the determination of one’s path and end through divine destiny.

Nevertheless, the apparent meaning concerns a denial in this life. God’s seal is a consequence of prior wrongdoing, not an initial act against people in this world; once they have denied, the seal fixes disbelief in their hearts and prevents receptivity to the messengers’ proofs. “Manifest proofs” includes all āyāt (signs and communications) brought as reminders: signs in the world, signs within people themselves, and prophetic miracles.

The commentary rejects several alternative readings. It finds unsupported the claim that their earlier disbelief merely continued from the beginning of the prophetic mission until their hostility became entrenched. It rejects the distinction between intuitive basic beliefs and detailed religious laws as contrary to the apparent meaning of takdhīb and the context. The proposal that they would disbelieve if destroyed and returned to life is called the least plausible. It finds no evidence for assigning “they had disbelieved” to forefathers and “they were not to believe” to descendants. Treating all generations as a single historical unit is valid in itself, but does not suit this context, where each town’s messengers apparently brought proofs in a single occurrence rather than through an ongoing series. The claim that bi-mā means “because of their earlier disbelief” is refuted by the parallel use of bihi and reduces to the first rejected view. Finally, interpreting earlier disbelief solely as pre-eternal denial of the covenant is true only as an inner layer, not the apparent meaning, because the verse itself makes sealing follow a wrongdoing committed in this life.

On verse (7:102), “covenant” means loyalty to and observance of a covenant, not merely its existence. It may mean God’s covenant through the pleasant and painful signs He sends, or the covenant people intuit through their intellects when they recognize their need for God and undertake to worship Him alone without partners. The transgression of most people is their failure to remain loyal to this covenant.

verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains that the elite’s claim that Moses sought to expel them from their land means that he would secure the support of the Children of Israel, take Egypt, end their independence, and exile them as conquering nations commonly exiled the defeated. Their advice to arjih Moses and Aaron means to defer action against them, rather than hastily kill them and risk being charged with injustice or cruelty, while sending emissaries through the towns to gather magicians capable of countering Moses’ sorcery. The variant recitation arjihi reflects a different grammatical treatment of the word, but the intended command remains to postpone action against Moses together with Aaron.

The narrative omits the intervening dispatch and summons for concision before stating that the magicians came to Pharaoh. Their request for a reward is phrased declaratively to stress the demand, although it may be understood as a question; the recitation attributed to Ibn ʿĀmir makes the question explicit. Pharaoh accepts their request and adds the inducement of proximity to himself. The magicians then offer Moses the choice of throwing first or allowing them to throw first. This reveals their preparedness, defiance, and confidence that they would prevail regardless of order, while the offer itself also carries an element of courtesy.

Moses tells them to throw. Their tremendous magic bewitched people’s eyes and terrified them. Here siḥr is an influence over perception by which people see what lacks external reality, and istirʿāb means frightening someone. God then directs Moses to throw down his staff. The statement implies that after the magicians had cast their things, Moses threw his staff; it became a snake and swiftly swallowed their fabrication. What they had faked was a distortion from its proper form and hence a falsehood.

The truth thereby became established and their sorcery was reduced to nothing. The image of truth “setting in” conveys its becoming firmly established after seeming, figuratively, like something suspended and uncertain whether it would settle. Pharaoh and his party were defeated at the great public gathering and departed humiliated.

The passive wording that the magicians “were cast down” in prostration emphasizes their overpowering encounter with Moses’ miracle. Although they prostrated of their own accord, they were so overwhelmed and helpless before the sign that it was as though they had been thrown down without awareness. Their confession of faith in the Lord of all worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron, establishes faith both in God and in Moses and Aaron as His messengers.

Al-Mizan does not accept the view that their mention of Moses and Aaron merely clarified that they did not mean Pharaoh by “the Lord of all worlds.” The polytheists did not understand lordship as one central authority owning, sustaining, and directing every realm; they divided the world among many lords and regarded God only as chief over the other lords and gods. Pharaoh’s statement, “I am your supreme lord” (79:24), claims superiority in meeting the particular needs of the Egyptians through his closeness to them, not governance of all worlds, though superstition could have led people to ascribe even that universal status to him.

Pharaoh rebukes the magicians with hubris and contempt for believing before his permission. His wording can be taken as a censuring statement or as a rhetorical question. He accuses them of conspiracy in the capital: before the summons they had been dispersed throughout the country and had not met Moses, so any alleged agreement must have arisen after their gathering in the city. According to his charge, they planned to seize the capital and expel its inhabitants. By presenting them as makers of mischief in the land (ifsād fī al-arḍ), he claims justification for exceptionally severe punishment. His declaration that they will soon know is a threat.

He then threatens, with repeated emphasis, to cut off a hand and foot on opposite sides—either the right hand with the left foot or the left hand with the right foot—and afterwards crucify them all. Crucifixion involved first torturing a criminal, then fastening him to wood and raising him publicly for others to see and take warning.

The magicians answer that Pharaoh resents nothing but their belief in their Lord’s signs. His threat does not constitute evil for them, as he assumes, because they will return to their Lord and live happily in His proximity; their response thus expresses belief in the afterlife. Their use of the plural “signs” indicates that they saw distinct signs in the staff’s becoming a python, swallowing their ropes and staffs one by one, and returning to its original form. Their only supposed offense is the faith for which Pharaoh hates them.

Instead of being frightened, they turn to God in a spiritually absorbed state. Their prayer, “Our Lord! Pour patience upon us,” asks for strength to bear the intended torture without disturbance or anxiety. The wording compares them to containers and patience to a liquid poured into them until full. Their request to die as submitters concerns the possibility that Pharaoh will kill them. Al-Mizan presents their direct, free, and courageous response to a powerful tyrant who claimed, “I am your supreme lord” (79:24), as an astonishing display of composed faith, knowledge, resolve, and noble moral character. Their speeches to Pharaoh in this sūrah, Sūrah Ṭā-Hā, and Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ are especially instructive, though a fuller treatment is beyond the present discussion.

verses.126:
Al-Mizan introduces this sequence as the beginning of the Moses narratives: his first appearance before Pharaoh to deliver the Children of Israel and his two signs, followed by his work among Israel, the afflictions and deliverance, the Torah and calf, and further instructive Israelite accounts.

Al-Mizan treats the distinctive introduction of Moses as deliberate emphasis. Moses was the third of the Resolute Messengers (ūlū al-ʿazm), bringing a scripture and a divine code of law (shariah), and his mission marks a further elaboration in the gradual development of divine religion after Noah and Abraham. The differing introductions of Noah, Hūd and Ṣāliḥ, Lot, Shuʿayb, and Moses indicate these stages: Hūd and Ṣāliḥ propagated Noah’s religion, Lot belonged to Abraham’s, and Moses brought a new scripture and law. Yet divine religion is one, and its codes do not contradict one another; they differ through concision, elaboration, addition, and perfection in accordance with humanity’s increasing capacity to receive divine teaching. When humanity reaches its highest intellectual development, the permanent Book and law are established and messengership and prophethood are sealed. Human growth thereafter continues through realizing, practicing, and spreading that religion in society.

The verse gives a concise overview of Moses’ story before its detailed account. More generally, these are stories of the communities to which prophets were sent: they rejected and denied the messengers and were ultimately exterminated by punishment. This accords with the chapter’s concern with humanity’s fidelity to the divine covenant, warning all people and reminding believers. Moses came after Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb, to the Egyptian ruler and his prominent courtiers. Firʿawn was a general title for Egyptian rulers, and the Qur’an does not name this Pharaoh. God’s signs apparently include Moses’ staff and white hand as well as the later distinct afflictions of flood, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood; Moses’ Qur’anic miracles are exceptionally numerous. Their wronging of the signs means rejecting and denying them. Their corruption included mischief and oppression of the Children of Israel, whose release Moses demanded.

Moses’ designation of God as the Lord of all worlds directly confronts polytheism’s belief in independent lords over separate portions of existence. His statement that he ascribes only truth to Allah emphasizes that he says nothing God did not charge him to say. The manifest proof from their Lord grounds his primary claim to be a messenger, from which his demand for Israel’s release follows. The expression ḥaqīq ʿalá may suggest particular eagerness and concern to speak only truth; the recitation ḥaqīq ʿalayya instead makes that truthfulness incumbent upon him. Pharaoh’s two conditional statements are not redundant: he demands production of the alleged sign while also revealing that he does not regard Moses as truthful.

Moses immediately answered by casting down his staff, which became a manifest thuʿbān, a huge snake. This does not conflict with the description of a jānn, a small snake, in the earlier encounter on Mount Ṭūr: the latter belonged to that earlier story, while the huge snake appeared before Pharaoh. Moses then drew his hand from his armpit. Although some narrations say it shone like the sun, the Qur’an describes only its whiteness; nevertheless, it was unmistakably supernatural to the onlookers.

The account then reports the deliberations of Pharaoh’s elite rather than Pharaoh’s own immediate words. They judged Moses an expert magician deceitfully seeking Israel’s release, so that the Israelites would support him in removing them from the land and abolishing their order. The verses portray their collective counsel: Pharaoh first raised the issue; the courtiers discussed it, endorsed his assessment, and recommended holding Moses and Aaron while gathering magicians to defeat magic with magic. Pharaoh accepted this advice and announced it to Moses. When the magicians arrived, the elite also consulted privately and agreed that they must confront him as a united force. Their allegation that Moses sought to expel them meant that, with Israel’s help, he aimed to seize Egypt, destroy their independence, and exile them, as conquering nations commonly did.

Their command to arjih Moses and Aaron means to postpone action rather than rush to kill them and incur the charge of injustice or cruelty, while dispatching military emissaries to summon magicians from the towns. The magicians’ arrival is concisely narrated after the omitted intervening summons. Their form of asking for a reward emphatically seeks it, though it may also be read as an explicit question, as in the recitation attributed to Ibn ʿĀmir. Pharaoh granted the reward and further promised them nearness to himself. Prepared and confident, the magicians gave Moses the choice of who would throw first; this was defiant confidence in their victory, though offering the choice also expresses courtesy.

Moses told them to throw. Their tremendous magic bewitched people’s eyes and frightened them: in this context, magic influences the senses so that people see what has no external reality. God then directed Moses to cast down his staff; after it became a snake, it swiftly swallowed what they had fabricated, that is, the false distortion produced by their sorcery. Thus the truth was established and their work was nullified. Pharaoh and his party were defeated before the great assembled crowd and withdrew abased.

The passive statement that the magicians “were cast down” depicts how overwhelmingly Moses’ sign affected them: though they themselves prostrated, they were so awestruck that they seemed not to know who had cast them down. Their prostration and confession of faith in the Lord of all worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron, therefore attest both belief in God and belief in Moses and Aaron as His messengers. Al-Mizan rejects the explanation that naming Moses and Aaron merely distinguished God from Pharaoh. Polytheists did not properly conceive a single Lord who owns, sustains, and directs all worlds; rather, they distributed existence among many lords, treating God as the Lord of lords. Pharaoh’s claim, “I am your supreme lord”, concerned his preeminent capacity to meet the Egyptians’ needs, not rule over all existence, although superstition might have led some to ascribe universal lordship to him.

Pharaoh’s response to the magicians is a contemptuous rebuke, whether read as a statement or a rhetorical question. He charges that their belief was a conspiracy devised in the capital, where they had gathered and first met Moses after previously being scattered through the country. He thus accuses them of plotting to seize the city and expel its people, classifying them as makers of mischief in the land and claiming a pretext for the harshest punishment. “Soon you will know” is a threat. He emphatically threatens to sever a hand and a foot from opposite sides, then crucify them all; crucifixion entailed torture, fastening the victim to wood, and raising him publicly as a warning.

The magicians answer that Pharaoh’s punishment cannot harm them as he supposes, because they will return to their Lord and live happily near Him. Their only alleged fault is faith in the signs of their Lord, and their statement thus shows belief in the afterlife. By using the plural “signs,” they regard the staff’s transformation, its swallowing of the ropes and staffs, and its return to its original form as distinct divine signs. Their prayer for patience asks God to grant them strength to endure Pharaoh’s intended torture without anxiety or disturbance; the image of pouring patience upon them likens them to vessels filled to the brim. Their request to die as submitters is made in case Pharaoh kills them. Rather than being intimidated by a tyrant who claimed, “I am your supreme lord”, they speak freely and courageously with faith, knowledge, composure, and resolve. Al-Mizan regards their direct address to Pharaoh, also narrated in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā and Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ, as richly instructive for its spiritual states and moral qualities, though a fuller discussion lies outside this work’s scope.

verses.137:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a synopsis of Moses’ mission in Egypt after he called Pharaoh and his clan to God and demanded the Israelites’ freedom. Moses showed successive miracles until God delivered him and his people, drowned Pharaoh and his hosts, and made the Children of Israel heirs to the east and west of the blessed land.

The commentary explains that Pharaoh’s elite sought to incite him to exterminate Moses and his people. Pharaoh’s answer rejects the need for total extermination because they already dominated the Israelites; instead, he would restore the former punishment of killing their sons and sparing their women as maidservants. His assertion of dominance both indicates that the elite had sought extermination in particular and calms their agitation. By mentioning Pharaoh’s gods, the elite further provoked him: Moses was disregarding both Pharaoh’s service and that of his gods.

Al-Mizan takes ālihataka to show that Pharaoh, despite claiming divinity and compelling his people to worship him, himself worshipped other gods. The objection is that his claims, “I am your supreme lord” and “I do not know of any god for you other than me,” appear to make him an atheist who commanded worship of himself alone; on this view, ālihataka may be read as ilāhatika, “your worship,” synonymous with ʿibādah. The commentary replies that Pharaoh’s exclusivist claim concerned the Egyptian public: he posed as the sole lord directing their affairs, not as one who denied every god governing his own affairs. This accords with polytheism, in which gods are directors of particular affairs rather than creators of heaven and earth. His statement that he did not know another god for his people negates his knowledge of one; it does not affirm that no others existed.

Al-Rāzī’s reported view is that Pharaoh could not rationally have believed himself creator of the heavens and earth, so was more likely an atheist who perhaps treated stars as determining the lower world while asserting his own authority within it; he could then have worshipped star-idols. Al-Mizan judges this confused: a lord or god for idolaters and star-worshippers was not necessarily the creator; atheists do not worship stars; and star-worshippers and Sabeans do not deny a creator. The correct view is that Pharaoh regarded himself as the exclusive lord of Egypt and its people, not as the sole creator. A translator’s note observes that the Qur’an does not otherwise mention Pharaoh’s gods or idols and reports a suggestion that the expression may refer to statues of Pharaoh erected for people elsewhere in Egypt to worship.

Moses’ command to seek Allah’s help and be patient urges the Israelites toward liberation from Pharaoh’s bondage and endurance under his threatened punishments. Pharaoh does not own the earth or control its benefits; it belongs to God, who grants its inheritance as He wills. For these people, taqwá consists in seeking God’s help and patiently remaining on His way, through which they may inherit land then held by Pharaoh’s clan. The unconditional statement that the outcome belongs to the Godwary expresses a divine custom: every species reaches the end and happiness for which it was created when it follows its proper course. Human beings likewise attain the good end by following their fiṭrah (primal nature, innate disposition, initial makeup), restraining themselves from transgressing God’s path, rejecting His signs, and causing corruption.

The Israelites’ complaint that they were tormented before and after Moses came means that his arrival had not yet ended their bondage and humiliation. Al-Mizan regards ityān and majīʾ here as synonymous variants for “coming,” rejecting the view that the former means Moses’ bringing miracles: it requires an unsupported omission and does not fit their complaint. A translator’s note nevertheless suggests that atá may mark setting out toward something, whereas jāʾa may mark arrival. Moses’ reply renews hope while keeping succession conditional: if they act with Godwariness, perhaps God will destroy their enemy and make them heirs, but dominion will test how they act. Thus God neither chooses nor honors them without a basis or condition. The commentary says this refutes the Jewish belief that the descendants of Jacob possess an inviolable, unconditional chosen status and irrevocable ownership of the Holy Land.

The droughts inflicted on Pharaoh’s clan were repeated years of famine and loss of produce, intended to awaken them. Pharaoh’s āl means those specially connected to him, namely the Egyptians other than the Israelites. The plural sinīn indicates separate droughts rather than one continuous famine, and the context indicates alternating periods of adversity and prosperity.

When prosperity returned after hardship, Pharaoh’s people claimed it as their own due; when misfortune came, they treated Moses and his followers as its evil omen. Their reaction shows that accustomed prosperity had made them regard abundance as normal and owed to them. The verse’s wording reflects this: idhā, “whenever,” and the definite al-ḥasanah portray good as their familiar norm, while in, “if,” and the indefinite sayyiʾah portray evil as exceptional. Taṭayyur means attributing ill luck to something, originally through omens associated with birds. Their actual ṭāʾir is their share of evil—God’s punishment, preserved against them by their deeds—though most do not know this. Al-Mizan considers the alternative interpretation of ṭāʾir as the record of deeds less suited to the context.

Their assertion that no sign could make them believe was meant to discourage Moses and mock his miracles as bewitchment: they called what he named signs mere magic. God then sent flood, locusts, qummal, frogs, and blood. Ṭūfān may mean any besieging event, though it commonly denotes abundant water or a land-covering flood. Qummal has been interpreted as large monkeys or tiny flies, and may alternatively be qaml, lice. The signs were mufaṣṣalāt, distinct and separately observable events, not simultaneous or accidental occurrences. The following verses show a recurring sequence: Moses warned of each punishment, they implored him to remove it and promised faith and the Israelites’ release, and then they violated their promise.

Rijz means punishment, specifically the punishment accompanying each of those signs. Their appeal to Moses by the covenant God had made with him means, in context, God’s commitment not to reject Moses’ prayer. In exchange for relief, they made a binding ʿahd: to believe and to let the Children of Israel leave with him. Al-Mizan reads the phrase about removal until an ajal as showing that this agreement had a fixed term, perhaps stipulated by Moses or by Pharaoh’s people; once relief was granted and the allotted time expired, they breached their contract with God and Moses. A translator’s note qualifies this reading: although ajal has a fixed technical legal sense, it often means an indeterminate limited period in the Qur’an; the apparent meaning may instead be that they remained lenient only for a while before returning to cruelty and defiance. Yamm simply means sea, in which God drowned them for denying and remaining oblivious to His signs.

The blessed land inherited by the previously abased Israelites apparently means the Levant, described from east to west, since the blessed land is the Holy Land around Palestine. Their abasement highlights God’s extraordinary raising and empowering of the weak. His “best word” is the decree, previously conveyed by Moses, to destroy their enemy and make them inherit the land; its fulfillment is the movement of that promise from potentiality into actuality, and their patience is given as its cause. Finally, tadmīr means annihilation: God destroyed what Pharaoh’s people made and built, whether their constructions and manufactures, their roofed buildings and palaces, or their trellised gardens.

verses.142: Al-Mizan states that Moses’ tryst lasted forty nights—thirty completed by ten more—and that he appointed Aaron his successor, commanding him to set matters right and avoid the corrupt.
verses.143: Al-Mizan recounts that Moses asked to look upon his Lord. Told that he could not see Him unless the mountain endured, Moses saw the mountain crumble at God’s disclosure and fell unconscious; recovering, he glorified God, repented, and declared himself first among the believers.
verses.144: Al-Mizan states that God chose Moses above the people through His messages and direct speech, and commanded him to receive this gift gratefully.
verses.145: Al-Mizan states that God inscribed advice and elaboration in the Tablets for Moses, commanding him to uphold them firmly, order his people to follow their best guidance, and warning that He would show the abode of transgressors.
verses.146: Al-Mizan states that God turns the unjustly proud from His signs: despite every sign, they disbelieve, reject rectitude, and adopt error because they deny and heedlessly neglect His signs.
verses.147: Al-Mizan states that those who deny God’s signs and the encounter of the Hereafter have their works annulled and are requited only for what they did.
verses.148: Al-Mizan recounts that, during Moses’ absence, his people worshiped a lowing calf made from their ornaments, though it neither spoke to them nor guided them; in doing so they were wrongdoers.
verses.149: Al-Mizan relates that, once they regretted their act and recognized their error, they pleaded for their Lord’s mercy and forgiveness lest they be losers.
verses.150: Al-Mizan recounts Moses’ angry return, his rebuke that his people had replaced him evilly and hastened their Lord’s decree, and his seizing Aaron by the head. Aaron pleaded that the people had overpowered him and nearly killed him, asking Moses not to count him among the wrongdoers.
verses.151: Al-Mizan relates Moses’ prayer that God forgive him and Aaron and admit them into His mercy, for He is the most merciful.
verses.152: Al-Mizan states that the calf-worshipers will meet their Lord’s wrath and abasement in this world; thus are fabricators requited.
verses.153: Al-Mizan states that those who commit evil but then repent and believe will thereafter find their Lord All-Forgiving and Ever-Merciful.
verses.154:
Al-Mizan treats these verses as a continuation of the chapter’s theme: nations generally resist the religious call and break God’s covenant, while God specially favors believers and punishes disbelievers. They recount Israel’s crossing of the sea, its request for an idol, its worship of the calf during Moses’ absence, and the revelation of the Torah.

The commentary explains that ʿukūf means turning to and adhering reverently to something. The Israelites’ request for a god meant a god fashioned for them like the idols fashioned for the people they encountered. Though descended from Abraham’s monotheistic religion and preceded by prophets such as Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, most Israelites had materialistic, sense-bound tendencies, reinforced by long residence under idolatrous Egyptians. They conceived God physically and repeatedly reduced Moses’ teaching of divine transcendence to imagined shapes. Moses therefore addressed their limited understanding: he condemned their ignorance, declared idol-worship fruitless, and described God through His attributes so that they would know He cannot be represented by an image.

“What they are in” denotes the idolaters’ path and tradition, and their “doing” their rites. Their path is destined for destruction and their religious works are void; intelligent people should instead serve God, whose worship yields enduring good. Moses’ question, “Shall I find you a god other than Allah?” means that any god he could manufacture or assign would be other than their true Lord. God’s having favored them over the nations identifies Him through His lordship, manifest signs, true religion, and deliverance from Pharaoh. Thus Moses’ concise answer meets the underlying idolatrous objection that an unseen God cannot be worshiped: He is worshiped through knowledge of His attributes.

The torment imposed by Pharaoh’s clan was humiliating and excessive: they repeatedly killed the Israelites’ sons and spared their women to serve them. The great test apparently refers to these afflictions. Although some exegetes take the address as directed to Jews living at the Qur’an’s revelation, Al-Mizan considers it more consistent with the context that Moses’ own companions are addressed in astonishment at their swift forgetfulness of this deliverance.

A mīqāt is a specified time assigned for an act, unlike waqt, the general time or duration of something. Moses’ tryst consisted of an initial thirty nights and a further ten, totaling forty; the reference to forty nights elsewhere states the total, while this verse gives its two stages. The appointment drew Moses near to God for remembrance and private discourse, for which night is especially fitting because the senses are less distracted and the soul readier for intimacy. The Torah was among the blessings of this nocturnal tryst.

Moses appointed Aaron as successor when departing, since succession presupposes the principal’s absence. His command to set things right and not follow the agents of corruption concerns government and social administration, not a warning against religious sin: Aaron was an infallible prophet and messenger. Moses directs him not to govern according to, or accept the counsel of, corrupt people among the community. The warning indicates that rebels and troublemakers were seeking to sabotage Moses’ work of order and unity and to divide the Israelites.

Al-Mizan first gives the apparent reading of Moses’ request to be shown God: being enabled to look precedes looking, which in turn precedes seeing. God’s “You shall never see Me” means that Moses could not bear the disclosure, as the test of the mountain shows. God disclosed Himself to the mountain, crushing it, and Moses fell dead or unconscious from the scene; when he regained consciousness, he repented of his request and professed belief that God cannot be seen.

The commentary then maintains that the request cannot concern bodily sight. Physical sight requires material conditions and an image corresponding to an object, whereas the Qur’an decisively teaches that God has no likeness, body, physical property, location, direction, or temporal and spatial limitation. No sensory or mental image can represent Him. Moses, one of the ūlū al-ʿazm and chief among prophets, could not have been ignorant of this; nor can divine omnipotence make a physical faculty perceive what is absolutely beyond matter and material properties. Therefore both Moses’ request and God’s answer concern a non-physical vision.

Verses that affirm seeing or encountering God must be read with those that deny sensory apprehension, such as The sights do not apprehend Him, yet He apprehends the sights (6:103). Some scholars explain ruʾyah as decisive knowledge, but Al-Mizan argues that not every certain knowledge is called seeing: certainty about historical persons, distant cities, self-evident propositions, or acquired concepts is knowledge, not ruʾyah. Ruʾyah properly applies to direct awareness of one’s own self and inner states—desire, aversion, love, hatred, hope, and the like—without inference, argument, sensory mediation, or a mental image. Knowledge of another’s inner state, by contrast, is inferred from observable conditions.

This direct, inner awareness is the vision meant in Qur’anic affirmations of divine vision. God’s witnessing and encompassing all things in (41:53-54) are not physical presence; consequently, the encounter with Him cannot be the meeting of two bodies in a shared place and time. “The heart did not deny what it saw” (53:11) attributes seeing to the rational soul, not the bodily organ. The stain caused by sin veils hearts from God, showing that the relevant vision is through the soul. The “eye of certainty” in (102:5-7) and Abraham’s vision of the malakūt, the inward orientation of things, likewise attest a seeing beyond physical sight.

Human beings possess a direct shuʿūr of their Lord besides belief acquired by proofs. This awareness is not destroyed; occupation with oneself and sin only bring ghaflah, heedlessness of a reality that remains present. The Qur’an and rational arguments support this, and Al-Mizan says the narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt confirm it. For righteous servants, this knowledge reaches its completion in the Hereafter: “Some faces will be fresh on that day, looking toward their Lord” (75:22-23). In this world the soul is occupied with bodily management and needs, while all are traveling and laboring toward the encounter with their Lord, realized after death. This special decisive knowledge is what the Qur’an calls ruʾyah and liqāʾ; whether those terms are literally or figuratively used is secondary to the contextual evidence. Al-Mizan holds that the Qur’an uniquely disclosed this extension of direct, presential knowledge from self-knowledge to knowledge of God.

Moses had already known God through His signs, then through election to messengerhood and direct speech; he sought the highest stage, knowledge through seeing. God’s everlasting negation applies to this worldly life, in which attachment to bodily life prevents complete severance from all besides God. It does not exclude the Hereafter, where other verses affirm such vision. The particle lan can negate something throughout worldly life without precluding a later end, and verses affirming the Hereafter’s vision may qualify its apparent absoluteness. The mountain test specifically concerns Moses’ capacity to endure divine manifestation, not the impossibility of manifestation itself: God did disclose Himself to the mountain, which thereby lost its identity as a mountain and was reduced to dust.

Moses’ swoon cannot be explained merely by the visual shock of the mountain’s collapse, for he had witnessed far more astonishing miracles without terror. It resulted from an experiential realization concerning his request and God’s absolute dominance, manifested to the mountain that could not remain even for a moment. His repentance accordingly acknowledges that the request was out of place in this world; tawbah here is return to God after any distance, not necessarily repentance for sin. “I am the first of the believers” most fittingly means the first among his people to believe that God cannot be seen in this worldly manner; the alternative that it merely means his prior faith is unlikely in context.

God’s choosing of Moses distinguishes His messages from His speech. The messages are the commands, prohibitions, teachings, wisdoms, and laws Moses had to convey, whether received through an angel, cast into his heart, or otherwise. Divine speech is direct communication without an angel. It is neither human conventional speech made of sound waves nor merely God’s creation of sounds, because sounds alone do not establish their intended meaning as God’s. Revelation instead involves a unique link between its recipient and the unseen, by which the recipient is certain of God’s intended meaning; this link may accompany sounds or occur otherwise. The verse displays God’s favor to Moses and tells him to be content with, receive gratefully, and not demand beyond this election.

The Tablets—the Torah—contained a selection of admonition and elaboration concerning the beliefs and practices needed by Moses’ people, not every religious teaching and law needed by humankind. Moses was commanded to hold them “with power,” meaning with resolute seriousness, and to command his people to hold to their best: to avoid evil, adhere to good, and prefer the better where good and better confront one another. The abode of transgressors is, in the flow of the passage, the end of those who violate this command and depart from guidance into evil and error; the following verse nearly interprets it. Other proposed readings identify it with hell, Pharaoh’s houses, the dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd, the towns of the Amalekites and others in the Levant, or a transgressing group that will rule over Israel.

Pride “in the earth” means seeking ascendancy over God’s servants through domination and enslavement, and is necessarily unjust. Thus “unjustly” is condemnatory and descriptive, not a restriction that would leave some such earthly pride rightful. Those characterized by it persist in denial even when shown every sign, deliberately reject the way of rectitude, and adopt error. Their conduct admits no excuse of ignorance or mistake; it arises from denial and heedlessness regarding God’s signs, which may also explain why God turns them away from those signs.

For deniers of the signs and the Hereafter’s encounter, deeds fail. Al-Mizan emphasizes that an act’s result is the act itself, and that ḥabṭ, the annulment of good acts, is itself returned to the agent as a result: evil deeds bring painful consequences, while annulled good acts yield no reward. Jazāʾ may here specifically mean reward; they have none because their good works have failed. The inference that neglecting an obligation deserves no punishment unless one commits a contrary sinful act is therefore false. The Qur’an establishes that disobeying God and His Messenger is itself sufficient for punishment.

The calf was an inanimate body made from the people’s ornaments that merely produced a bovine sound. Their worship of it during Moses’ absence is censured by the immediate rational criterion that a god must communicate what pleases it and guide its servants to the way of worship. The calf neither spoke nor guided. The Israelites already knew that God had spoken to and guided Moses, and through him had guided them; if the calf had been the God of Moses as claimed, it too should have spoken and guided. Its lack of these primary marks of divinity made their worship plainly irrational, and their adoption of it is attributed to their wrongdoing.

Their subsequent remorse means that they came to recognize what they had neglected and realized their error, as though their failed work had been returned and placed before them for inspection. Majmaʿ al-bayān explains the underlying expression as a figurative usage for such regret and discovery of a hidden fault; Al-Mizan regards this the most plausible explanation among the many proposed interpretations. Their plea for mercy and forgiveness expresses that remorse. Although they realized their error after Moses’ return, their regret is placed directly after the account of the calf for coherence; its prayer is also separated from Moses’ later prayer, since the Israelites’ prayer is not at the same level as that of Moses and Aaron.

Moses returned already informed of the people’s deviation, but direct observation brought the outward expression of anger that bare knowledge had not. Knowledge can cause inward grief and resentment, whereas seeing a violation arouses the defensive faculty into verbal or physical response. He rebuked them for replacing him evilly and for seeking their Lord’s decree—the Torah’s revelation—before its appointed time, as though their impatience could alter a matter governed solely by divine wisdom. Other proposed meanings of their haste include rushing to worship the calf before divine command, impatience for promised reward, impatience with the command to wait for Moses and keep his covenant, or changing the covenant because they considered the tryst overdue; Al-Mizan finds its own reading most suited to the context.

Moses threw down the Tablets and seized Aaron by the hair, believing Aaron had not resisted the people sufficiently and had relied on his own judgment despite the instruction to set things right and avoid the corrupt. Aaron invoked their mother to soften Moses, explained that the people had overpowered him and nearly killed him because he opposed the calf, and asked not to be treated as one of the wrongdoers. Aaron had also feared that leaving them would produce division among the Israelites. The differing judgment of the two infallible prophets is a difference in personal orientation and assessment of expediency, not disobedience to a divine command. Moses’ action was disciplinary in relation to an advisory command, not punishment for violating an authoritative command; Aaron was in fact right, and Moses excused him after hearing his account. Explanations that Moses only acted out of general rage, wished to display anger to the people, drew Aaron close for a private question, or comforted him are judged mostly or wholly incongruous with the context.

Moses then prayed, “My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy,” and the scope of forgiveness, Al-Mizan notes, is not confined to sins. Those who worshiped the calf are threatened with immense, unspecified wrath and abasement in worldly life. This may refer to their ensuing punishment, to the later humiliation, poverty, killing, exile, and enslavement of the Israelites, or to a punishment extending to the Hereafter as well. Whatever precise outcome is intended, the verse establishes a recurring divine custom: fabricators of lies meet wrath and abasement in this life.

The promise that those who commit evil, then repent and believe, find God All-Forgiving and Ever-Merciful is both general and an exception for calf-worshipers. Genuine repentance for any sin cannot be prevented from acceptance. The repeated “after that” first refers to after wrongdoing and then to after repentance. The statements about requiting fabricators and the Prophet’s Lord form a digression addressed to the Prophet while recounting a past, ongoing event. Finally, once Moses’ anger subsided, he took up the Tablets, whose inscriptions contained guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord with rahbah: fear joined to precaution.
verses.155: Al-Mizan recounts that Moses chose seventy men for God’s tryst. When an earthquake seized them, he appealed to God not to destroy the people for the deed of their fools, calling the event a divinely willed trial through which He guides or leads astray. Invoking God as their Master and the best of forgivers, Moses asked for forgiveness and mercy.
verses.156:
Al-Mizan presents a plea that God decree goodness in this world and the Hereafter for those who have returned to Him. God replies that, while He visits punishment on whomever He wills, His mercy embraces all things; He will prescribe that mercy for those who are Godwary, give alms, and believe in His signs.

The passage identifies a decisive instance of such belief: following the Messenger, the unschooled prophet, whose description is found in the Torah and the Gospel. He enjoins right, forbids wrong, permits good things, prohibits vicious things, and removes burdens and shackles. Felicity belongs to those who believe in, honor, and help him, and follow the light sent down with him.
verses.157:
Al-Mizan explains that the burdens (iṣr) and shackles (aghlāl) removed by the Prophet are restraints that bind people and hold them back from good and reward, not merely physical weights. The verse presents eight identifying qualities of Prophet Muḥammad: he is a Messenger, unschooled, and a prophet; he enjoins right and forbids wrong; he makes good things lawful and vicious things unlawful; and he removes the burdens and shackles imposed on earlier communities. These characteristics, including the first three by which the People of the Book would recognize him, are said to be recorded in the Torah and Gospel.

The verse is an interpretation of “those who believe in Our signs” in (7:156), but it does not limit the preceding, more general promise of special mercy to Israelites who lived to follow Muḥammad. Rather, it extracts and highlights one particular application: when Muḥammad’s mission has appeared, belief in God’s signs requires the People of the Book to accept him. The earlier righteous followers of Moses and Jesus remain included in the broader category of those who believed and were Godwary. At the time of Muḥammad, Israelites who follow him have believed in Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad; in their miracles, laws, and obligations; and in the scriptural indications of Muḥammad’s prophethood and mission.

Replacing “believe” with “follow” teaches that real belief in divine signs is practical submission and obedience. Abstract assent without obedience is effectively denial. The descriptions of the Messenger are likewise signs of his truth found in earlier revelation. Although earlier religions and their righteous followers shared aspects of enjoining good, forbidding evil, permitting good things, prohibiting foul things, and relieving restrictions, Al-Mizan maintains that their perfection is exclusive to Islam. Islam gave commanding right and forbidding wrong the full force of jihād with wealth and life; comprehensively classified human conduct into lawful good and unlawful foul; and abrogated the burdens imposed upon the People of the Book, especially the Jews, along with obligations adopted by their scholars and innovations of priests and monks.

These five qualities together mean that the Prophet confirms and perfects the divine laws and teachings already found in the Torah and Gospel. Their full realization in his religion is itself evidence of his truthfulness, even apart from its foretold descriptions, because they constitute what a true religion must establish. The wording is broader than simply saying that he confirms previous scripture because the verse addresses all people, not only the People of the Book.

Taʿzīr means supporting the Prophet with honor and respect. The “light” sent down with him is the Qur’an, which illuminates the way of life and the path to happiness and perfection. Its being sent down “with him” indicates accompaniment: the Qur’an accompanies the Prophet as a sign and proof of his truth, since it manifests the perfection of previous divine religions and identifies him as the promised messenger. Al-Mizan rejects explanations that make “with him” refer to an omitted mission, to the followers, to the Prophet’s own following of the Qur’an, or that replace its meaning with “upon” or “at.” The verse’s conclusion shows that genuine following consists in faith in the Prophet’s mission, honoring and aiding him, and following God’s Book and its teachings; such people are the felicitous.

Al-Mizan then reads (7:158) as the direct universalization of this mission. Having established the Prophet’s religion as providing the right, prohibiting wrong, allowing good, forbidding foul, and lifting burdens, God commands him to declare himself Messenger to all humankind. God’s possession of the kingdom of the heavens and earth, His exclusive divinity, and His giving of life and death establish both that He may appoint Muḥammad and that He may send him to every people. This removes prejudices that denied the possibility of a messenger from another nation, whether Israelite assumptions of exclusive election and exemption from duty toward gentiles, or non-Arab resistance to an Arab prophet.

God’s giving life and death also means that He can grant the genuinely living state of happiness and guidance, while wretchedness and error are a real death. The command to believe in Allah and His Messenger and to follow the unschooled prophet is consequently framed in the third person as the Prophet’s conclusion from these proofs: he is the Messenger promised in the Torah and Gospel, who believes in Allah and all His words, including the laws and teachings sent to him and earlier prophets. The promised guidance is guidance to final happiness—Paradise and God’s satisfaction—not merely initial direction to the path, since faith and following have already been commanded. It is thus equivalent to the felicity promised in the preceding verse.

On (7:159), Al-Mizan notes the Qur’an’s fairness: after censuring Israelite sins, it praises a community among Moses’ people who guides by truth and judges justly through it. This likely refers to the prophets and Imams who came after Moses, because guidance by the truth and judgment through it in their full sense belong only to a divinely appointed prophet or Imam.

On (7:160), sibṭ, though literally a grandchild, means an Israelite tribe; the Israelites were divided into twelve tribal communities. Moses struck the rock at God’s command, and twelve springs emerged, one for each tribe and its allotted drinking place. The separate springs apparently prevented rivalry and dispute. Al-Mizan treats inbijās as synonymous with infijār, while noting the reported distinction that the former can indicate a gentle initial flow and the latter a copious outpouring. The verse also recalls the cloud shade, manna, and quails, and concludes that their wrongdoing harmed not God but themselves. The commentary places these events within the broader catalogue of Moses’ signs: the staff-serpent and white hand, the plagues upon Pharaoh’s people, the sea’s splitting, the death and restoration of the seventy, water from the rock, clouds, manna and quails, the mountain raised above Israel, God’s speech with Moses, the Torah’s revelation, and the transformation of some transgressors into apes.
verses.158: Al-Mizan declares the Messenger’s mission universal: he is sent to all humankind by the sole God, Who possesses the heavens and the earth and gives life and death. People are therefore commanded to believe in Allah and His unschooled Messenger, who believes in Allah and His words, and to follow him in order to be guided.
verses.159: Al-Mizan says that among Moses’ people, a community guides by truth and judges justly by it.
verses.160:
Al-Mizan introduces these Israelite accounts as signs specially bestowed to lead them to truth and taqwá, though their denial of the signs wronged only themselves. It explains that Moses’ selection of seventy men for the tryst implies a momentous but otherwise unspecified event, and that the earthquake was punishment for a grave sin. Moses’ words show that it caused their death.

The commentary identifies the rajfah, “earthquake,” with a ṣāʿiqah, “thunderbolt,” rather than an inward bodily tremor. It infers this by comparing the account with the Israelites’ demand to see God visibly and their subsequent restoration to life, and with passages that use rajfah and ṣāʿiqah for the destruction of Ṣāliḥ’s people. Verse (4:153) further indicates that the demand to see God concerned the revelation of the Book and preceded worship of the calf. Al-Mizan therefore considers it likely that Moses took the seventy to Mount Ṭūr to receive the Torah; although they apparently already believed in Moses’ prophethood, they demanded visible sight of God in order to verify the Torah’s divine origin.
