They were struck dead, restored through Moses’ prayer, and the later events—including the calf—followed. It notes that some narrations from the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt support this reconstruction.

Nevertheless, the verse’s chief purpose is simply to show that the Israelites wronged themselves, God punished them, and Moses prayed for them; it does not itself establish whether this was part of the preceding tryst narrative or an independent event. The commentary rejects proposed alternatives—three wholly separate episodes, a later penitential journey after calf-worship, the episode concerning an accusation that Moses killed Aaron, or an independent occurrence of the visible-sight demand—as unsupported, particularly by Qur’anic evidence or reliable hadith. The objection that the Qur’an cannot interrupt and resume one story mistakes its character: it is a book of guidance and wisdom, not a storybook. Nor does “what the fools amongst us have done” rule out a sinful demand made in speech, since disobedient speech is itself an act; indeed, the alternative accounts likewise make speech the cause of the quake. Thus the interpretation connecting the event to the earlier tryst remains most plausible.

Moses’ real, unspoken request was that the seventy be restored to life, lest Israel accuse him of having killed its elite, fall into apostasy, and thereby frustrate his mission. He prepares this petition by invoking divine Lordship, will, mercy, and forgiveness. “Had You willed” acknowledges that the matter rests wholly in God’s decision, while “and me before” means that an earlier destruction would have spared Moses the people’s accusations. His courteous question, “Will You destroy us because of what the fools amongst us have done?” appeals to the divine mercy and to God’s customary refusal to punish a people for the act of its fools.

Fitnah here means a test, and bihā refers to that test. The event is an instance of the universal trials through which guidance or error becomes actual, not a sign that God hastens to annihilate everyone who fails. Moses’ appeal therefore rests on the precedence of mercy over wrath and on God’s promise to support his mission. Calling God waliyyunā invokes His exclusive mastership, and ending with “the best of forgivers” frames the request for forgiveness and mercy. Moses names no resurrection explicitly, out of humility and ḥayāʾ, but Al-Mizan holds that it is contained in this prayer: the Qur’an says elsewhere that they were raised after death, and their restoration would not occur without Moses’ intercession or forgiveness of the sin for which they died.

In the next prayer, uktub means a definite divine decree and hudnā means that “we have returned.” Moses asks for the good life of this world and the Hereafter, grounding the request in returning to God, following His path, and adhering to fiṭrah. This return explains the request for goodness, whereas the preceding request for forgiveness was justified by God’s mastership and surpassing forgiveness.

God’s answer distinguishes punishment from mercy. Punishment is qualified by “whomever I will” because it is elicited by the recipient’s ingratitude and sin; it is not God’s initiating disposition or a necessity of Lordship. In its reality, punishment is non-existential: the withholding of mercy and blessing when a person lacks the capacity to receive them. Mercy, by contrast, issues directly from God’s Lordship and actually encompasses all things. Every existent is mercy, either for itself or, even where it is painful to it, through benefits accruing to other beings. Thus divine mercy embraces believers and unbelievers, sentient and non-sentient beings, this world and the Hereafter; beyond a “thing” is only non-existence.

Al-Mizan distinguishes this universal mercy from particular mercy. Universal mercy gives beings their existence, sustenance, and continuance. Particular mercy is the rewarding gift reserved for righteous believers: a luminous, blessed life in this world and God’s pleasure and Paradise in the Hereafter. Disbelievers and sinners have no share in it. Punishment—distress or extermination in this world, and Hell in the Hereafter—is the opposite of particular mercy, not of universal mercy. Relative descriptions of mercy and punishment may contrast peace with affliction or possession with deprivation, but both conditions remain within absolute universal mercy. Accordingly, “My mercy embraces all things” is unconditional actuality, not an omitted qualification by “whomever I will.”

The prescription of mercy for the Godwary, those who give alms, and believers in the signs is the consequent prescription of particular mercy. It is stated generally, not only about Moses’ people. It qualifies rather than rejects Moses’ petition: his return to God amounts to īmān, while God teaches that lasting qualification also requires taqwá—abstaining from the prohibited and observing obligations—and belief in the divine signs. Alms are obligatory financial dues, or spending in God’s way, rather than merely moral self-purification. Belief in the signs includes submission to the prophets, their miracles, revealed laws, and the signs establishing the truth of their missions, including the indications of Muḥammad in earlier scriptures.

The commentary therefore rejects the claim that Moses’ request was refused or granted only to Muḥammad’s community. Both parts of his prayer were accepted: the request for worldly and otherworldly good was granted with added conditions, and the earlier plea for forgiveness was accepted implicitly, as confirmed by the seventy’s resurrection. Finally, the shift from the majestic plural to God’s singular speech marks His personal attention to the intimate prayers of His servants. The return to “Our signs” then subtly links the discourse with the following verse, while preserving the distinction between God’s private answer to Moses and the broader thread of the passage.
verses.161: Al-Mizan recounts that they were told to settle in the town, eat freely, seek relief from sins, and enter its gate prostrating, so that their iniquities might be forgiven and the virtuous enhanced.
verses.162: Al-Mizan states that the wrongdoers altered the words they had been commanded to say, and a plague from heaven was sent against them because of their persistent wrongdoing.
verses.163: Al-Mizan recounts the story of a seaside town that violated the Sabbath: its fish appeared visibly on the shore on the Sabbath but not on other days. This was a test imposed because of their transgressions.
verses.164: Al-Mizan relates that the advisers of those whom Allah will punish justified warning them as an excuse before their Lord and in hope they might restrain themselves.
verses.165: Al-Mizan states that when they disregarded what they had been reminded of, God delivered those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers with a terrible punishment for their transgressions.
verses.166: They defiantly violated the prohibition and were told, “Be you spurned apes.”
verses.167: Al-Mizan recounts that the Lord proclaimed that, until the Day of Resurrection, He would send against them those who would inflict terrible punishment. Yet He is swift in retribution and is also All-Forgiving, Ever-Merciful.
verses.168: Al-Mizan states that God dispersed them into communities throughout the earth, some righteous and others otherwise, and tested them with good and bad times so that they might return.
verses.169: Al-Mizan describes an evil successor generation that inherited the Book but seized transient worldly gain, claiming they would be forgiven and repeatedly taking similar gain whenever it came to them. Although they had studied the Book and were bound by its covenant to ascribe only truth to Allah, they ignored that the Hereafter is better for the Godwary.
verses.170: Al-Mizan states that God does not waste the reward of those who hold fast to the Book, maintain the prayer, and set things right.
verses.171:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as further accounts of the Children of Israel’s breach of God’s commands and covenant. Their wrongdoing brought its consequences: punishment, the dominance of people who inflicted severe suffering, and, in later generations, an inheritance of the Book combined with selling God’s signs for paltry worldly gain. Only a few did not overstep the truth.

The town in (7:161) was in the Holy Land. The Israelites were ordered to enter it, fight the Amalekites, and drive them out, but they defied the command and left it to Moses, for which they were afflicted with the wilderness. They were commanded to seek relief from their sins and enter the gate prostrating. The promise to enhance the virtuous answers the implied question of what lies beyond forgiveness.

In the seaside town, the Sabbath prohibition concerned fishing. Fish from their region appeared visibly and near the shore on Saturdays, when fishing was forbidden, but did not appear in this way on other days, when fishing was permitted. Al-Mizan takes this unequal availability as a divine trial brought on by their widespread transgression: greed moved them to fish despite God’s command, since they lacked sufficient taqwá, or Godwariness and self-restraint.

The people divided into those who violated the Sabbath, those who admonished them, and apparently pious people who did not themselves disobey but neither forbade the evil nor separated from its perpetrators. The latter asked why the offenders were advised when God would destroy or severely punish them. The admonishers had two reasons: to establish their excuse before God by dissociating themselves from the evil, and to preserve the remaining hope that the offenders, or at least some of them, might desist or lessen their transgression.

“Forgetfulness” in (7:165) does not mean literal oblivion, for an actually forgetful person is not subject to religious duties and penalties. It means that the divine reminder had become ineffective. A person who persists in sin rather than repenting first feels inward pain, self-reproach, and constriction; but repeated sin strengthens its hold while weakening the reminder in the conscience, until the reminder’s presence makes no difference. Al-Mizan concludes that only those who forbade evil were delivered, while both the Sabbath-breakers and those who merely objected to admonishing them were seized, because the latter neither advised the sinners nor withdrew from them.

The commentary draws from this a general divine pattern: one must first try to stop wrongdoing; if unable, one must advise and admonish; and if this proves impossible or ineffective, one must migrate from or keep apart from the wrongdoers. Failure to undertake any of these stages makes one their partner and accomplice, exposed to the same severe seizure.

The defiance in (7:166) is extreme disobedience. Al-Mizan understands an omitted “refraining” in the phrase: they defiantly refused to refrain from what they had been forbidden. The command to become “spurned apes” signifies becoming outcast and driven away.

God’s proclamation in (7:167) is a sworn declaration that, for as long as the world endures, He will raise people over those wrongdoers to inflict terrible punishment on them. God’s swiftness in retribution concerns certain punishments that rapidly seize transgressors. The concluding names All-Forgiving and Ever-Merciful show that He is not always swift to punish: He is compassionate and forgiving, but some transgression and defiance make punishment definite, leaving no obstacle to its swift arrival.

Their dispersion into communities throughout the earth included righteous people and others who were not. Their “good” and “bad” times are worldly fortune and misfortune, by which they were tested so that they might return.

The later evil generation inherited the Book—its teachings, laws, admonitions, and lessons—yet immersed themselves in immediate and unstable worldly pleasures, whether sinful gains were small or great. The expression for the lower world underscores its inferiority and worthlessness. Their claim, “It will be forgiven us,” had no basis: it arose from pride in lineage, not a plan to repent or genuine hope in God’s forgiveness. True hope necessarily includes fear of its opposite; their claim instead served as self-exoneration, allowing them to continue in pleasure without guilt. It was a false wish and a temptation from Satan.

Their continual seizure of every similar gain confirms that they never repented or refrained from their wrongdoing. They had studied the Book and knew that their claim to forgiveness was unwarranted, despite the covenant that they would attribute nothing but truth to Allah. They nevertheless persisted in disobedience and undermined religion, even though the Hereafter, with its everlasting pleasures and freedom from evil, is better for the Godwary.

Holding fast to the Book and maintaining prayer characterize those who set things right. Prayer is singled out because it is a pillar of religion that preserves remembrance of God and humility before Him, the living spirit of religious laws and rites. Iṣlāḥ, setting things right, is the opposite of corruption in the earth and human society, which results from departure from fiṭrah, the divine intuition on which humankind was originated.

According to Al-Mizan, all divine scriptures convey religion in accordance with the capacities and conditions of their peoples, and are founded on this fiṭrah. Islām here means taslīm, submission to God’s customs in creation (takwīn), on which His laws of legislation (tashrīʿ) rest. Following religion therefore harmonizes human life with the realities and laws of existence and enables human development according to its true nature. That nature requires humility before the transcendent Origin of existence, sustenance, and success, as well as conformity of life to the laws governing existence.

Iṣlāḥ is consequently intrinsic to islām, not an optional result added to it. It straightens every aspect of life, purifies it of superstitions, and removes the burdens imposed by illusion and desire. Religious laws are not conventional commands first imposed and only afterward alleged to promote human welfare; they inherently incorporate the interests of people in this world and the Hereafter. The view that religion is merely arbitrary restraint, with no connection to creation or human well-being and with reward and punishment only externally decreed after death, is ignorance of religious teaching and a false accusation against its divine Prescriber. A divine book is identified by laws that serve both individual and social interests, and submission to it is submission to what God’s creation itself requires. Although the verse independently applies to followers of every divine scripture, its context primarily concerns the Children of Israel; the Book is thus the Torah, or the Torah and Gospel.

Finally, the mountain was plucked up by its roots and held over the Children of Israel like a canopy, which they thought was about to fall upon them. They were commanded to hold firmly to what they had been given and remember what it contained so that they might become Godwary. The passage identifies this as the raising of Mount Ṭūr above them.
verses.172: Al-Mizan states: God took the descendants of Adam from their loins, made them testify that He is their Lord, and received their acknowledgment. Thus, on the Day of Resurrection, they cannot plead ignorance of His Lordship or excuse their polytheism by claiming that they merely followed their fathers.
verses.173: Al-Mizan states: God took the descendants of Adam from their loins, made them testify that He is their Lord, and received their acknowledgment. Thus, on the Day of Resurrection, they cannot plead ignorance of His Lordship or excuse their polytheism by claiming that they merely followed their fathers.
verses.174:
Al-Mizan reads the covenant in these verses as a real disclosure of divine Lordship to every human being, but not as a second physical life occurring earlier in time. “Taking” the descendants from the Children of Adam and from their loins describes the differentiation of persons through generation: what begins as part of a parent is separated, completed, and made an independent human being, from whom another is then taken, until every person stands distinct and bears the consequences of his or her own acts. God then makes them witnesses over themselves. To make someone witness is to bring the person to the reality itself and show it directly, and the question “Am I not your Lord?” specifies what they are shown.

Every person can find this Lordship in the reality of the self. However proud or powerful someone appears, no one owns the self independently, can prevent death and misfortune at will, or manages life without relying on means that are themselves dependent. Need, poverty, and weakness belong to human existence itself and point immediately to the Owner and Director upon whom it depends. The witnessing is therefore not merely knowledge of an abstract proposition but a direct awareness of one’s own dependent reality. The answer, “Yes indeed! We bear witness,” acknowledges what has been shown. Divine speech need not consist of sounds: God’s purposeful act of giving existence can communicate His intended meaning, and the human response can likewise be real, conscious communication without being ordinary verbal conversation.

The covenant closes two possible excuses on the Day of Resurrection. Had no one been made to witness, all could claim complete ignorance of God’s Lordship and therefore exemption from responsibility. Had only earlier generations witnessed, later generations could say that their fathers knowingly introduced polytheism while they merely inherited it without access to the truth. By making every distinct person witness, God’s proof encompasses both fathers and descendants. Knowledge of the self’s dependence on its Lord is intrinsic rather than an empirical discovery accumulated through civilization, so it does not develop only after other forms of knowledge as inherited sciences do.

One group of exegetes interprets the entire event as the ordinary course of worldly life. On this account, God brings people from their parents, equips them to recognize their weakness and the signs of unity, and thereby asks through the language of their condition, “Am I not your Lord?” Their dependent state answers, “Yes.” These exegetes reject narrations about a pre-existent ʿālam al-dharr in which Adam’s descendants were extracted as tiny particles, made into rational witnesses, and returned to the loins. They argue that accountable witnesses would have to remember the event; universal forgetting is implausible and would open the door to reincarnation theories; the verse speaks of the loins and descendants of the Children of Adam rather than only Adam’s loin; its reference to polytheist fathers does not fit an undifferentiated gathering; forgotten pre-existence would still leave people dependent on fallible worldly reasoning; and a symbolic reading of the verse does not establish a literal prior event from disputed reports.

Hadith scholars and other proponents answer that loss of the scene’s details does not annul the covenant so long as the soul retains its fundamental knowledge of God’s Lordship. Mass forgetting is not logically impossible, and accepting it does not by itself prove transmigration. They take the sequence of descendants to include Adam’s immediate children and every later generation, read the excuse about the fathers as a collective human argument rather than one made by each individual, and maintain that a merely possible symbolic interpretation cannot displace the apparent meaning. They also deny that all relevant narrations are weak, noting that some are transmitted as authentic or reliable.

Al-Mizan concludes that the dispute has been framed incorrectly. The common narration-based particle theory imagines that Adam’s material seed was successively divided into every future person; each particle became a complete, intelligent human with hearing, sight, choice, and responsibility; all acknowledged Lordship, some sincerely and some inwardly disbelieving; and all were then returned through the sequence of loins while retaining only a basic knowledge of God. This construction is impossible. A material particle transmitted through ancestors is not the human person whose soul comes into being with that person’s bodily creation. Such a particle cannot simply be credited with the later person’s consciousness, cognition, covenant, reward, or punishment.

The theory also fails to explain how binding knowledge and responsibility arise. Human judgments presuppose concepts acquired through inner and outer perception in a developed embodied life. If God’s proof depends on the entire witnessing and covenant, forgetting them destroys the proof. If bare knowledge of Lordship alone suffices, fetuses, infants, those without reason, and the ignorant would all be fully accountable. If the covenant became binding through mature reason in the earlier world, then lost that force and became binding again when reason matured here, the first completion was unnecessary: both practical reason and recognition of Lordship can develop through worldly experience. Practical reason in particular grows through social life, emotion, benefit and harm, repeated choice, and success or failure—conditions absent from the supposed particle realm.

If those conditions are added to the earlier realm, it becomes another complete physical world containing prophecy, belief, disbelief, and action like this one. It would then require an earlier covenant-world to ground responsibility in it, producing the same problem again. The theory also claims universal necessity while exempting Adam and Eve, who had no atomic existence in another person’s loin; if their completed creation allowed them to know God here, the same can occur for their descendants upon maturity. In its temporal form, the theory makes every individual exist twice with the same worldly personality before completing the natural course, effectively making each person both identical with and other than himself or herself. Authentic revelation cannot require an impossibility, and a meaning inferred from a narration may not be imposed upon the Qur’an without testing whether the verse supports it.

Yet the worldly-only interpretation also fails. The verse’s use of idh, “when,” places the covenant in a stage preceding the present address; it does not naturally describe an event continuously unfolding in the same worldly life as the audience. That interpretation also reduces witnessing to indirect rational recognition and turns the narrated question and answer into an unintended language of condition. The text instead presents direct witnessing and a real exchange.

Al-Mizan resolves the problem by distinguishing temporal precedence from ontological precedence. The Qur’an allows one person to exist across different realms governed by different laws, as in worldly life, barzakh, and resurrection, without multiplying the person into separate identities. It also teaches that created things have unmeasured stores with God from which their delimited worldly existence descends, and that temporal becoming proceeds from the immediate divine command “Be.” Every created thing consequently has two inseparable aspects: a worldly aspect that unfolds gradually through time, change, potentiality, and acquired perfection, and a divine aspect facing God that is non-temporal, non-gradual, and present with all its properties at once.

Humanity in this divine aspect has an assembled existence with God. Individuals remain distinct, yet none is absent from another or from the Lord who gives them existence. This is their malakūt: not an earlier material population but the divine face of the same human reality, which ontologically precedes and encompasses its temporal unfolding. There people witness themselves as directly dependent on their sole Lord, not by inference through faculties that develop later. Because they are not veiled from Him, they consciously acknowledge His Lordship; polytheism and sin belong to the worldly aspect in which occupations, desires, time, and space obscure that original witnessing.

The covenant verse elaborates this higher plane in the language of descendants being distinguished, made witnesses over themselves, addressed, and answering. The precedence is like that of “Be” over temporal becoming, not one date before another. The witnessing keeps its direct meaning and the speech remains intentional and real, though not necessarily vocal. Narrations are compatible with the verse insofar as they affirm another plane of human existence or say that Adam was shown the malakūt of his descendants, just as Abraham was shown the malakūt of the heavens and earth; they do not justify the duplicated physical particle-world construction.

During worldly life people ordinarily know through concepts and reasoning and are distracted from this immediate knowledge. At resurrection, when the world’s veils and occupations are removed, they recover the original observation and remember what passed between them and their Lord. No generation can then plead either total unawareness or helpless imitation of polytheist ancestors. The final statement, “Thus do We elaborate the communications,” means that God distinguishes and clarifies His signs so their meanings are not confused. Their return from falsehood to truth is one purpose of that elaboration among other lofty purposes left unstated.
verses.175: Al-Mizan relates the case of one given God’s signs who cast them off; Satan then pursued him, and he became one of the perverse.
verses.176: Al-Mizan says that God could have raised him through the signs, but he attached himself to the earth and followed base desires. Like a dog that lolls out its tongue whether attacked or left alone, deniers persist in denial; these narratives are recounted so that people may reflect.
verses.177: Those who deny God’s signs wrong themselves, and their parable is evil.
verses.178: Al-Mizan states that those whom Allah guides are rightly guided, while those He leads astray are the losers.
verses.179:
Al-Mizan introduces these verses as the story of Balaam son of Beor, intended to show that apparent means of salvation do not save unless God wills salvation for a person. God does not will felicity for one engrossed in earthly life and following desire; such a person ends in hell. Their distinguishing mark is that they do not use heart, sight, and hearing in a beneficial way, which is heedlessness.

The commentary explains that nabaʾ is significant news, while ītāʾ here is the bestowal of spiritual signs and inner stations that illuminate knowledge of God and disclose the truth without doubt. Insilākh, literally emerging from a skin, depicts the divine signs as an outer cast from which the person’s inward evil comes away. Itbāʾ means following in another’s footsteps. Ghayy and ghawāyah suggest forgetting the intended goal, whereas ḍalāl more specifically describes one who remembers the destination but misses the route; in this verse, after casting off the signs and being pursued by Satan, the person has lost the right path and cannot escape perdition. The terms may also be used interchangeably for departure from the path to one’s goal.

Although exegetes differ over the identity of this man, the verse itself does not name him. Al-Mizan holds that its concise account plainly concerns a real event, not a merely symbolic story. It may be addressed to the Children of Israel or to all people: God had unveiled signs and spiritual indications to him, but he abandoned them, whereupon Satan pursued him until he could no longer save himself.

To cling to the earth is to adhere constantly to it, metaphorically to hanker after worldly pleasure and become absorbed in it; lahth describes a dog’s tongue hanging out from thirst. The pronoun in “by their means” refers to the divine signs. Being raised by them means drawing near to God and rising above the base life of this world. Such signs are outward instruments of guidance, but they do not independently ensure felicity, since their full effect depends on God’s will. God does not will felicity for one who turns away from Him for what distracts from Him and His abode of grace. Turning away and denying the signs are forms of ẓulm, and God does not guide the wrongdoing lot; those who deny His signs are destined for the Fire.

Thus the man was not raised because he chose attachment to earth and base desire, qualifying for misguidance rather than guidance. His likeness to a dog means that denial has become a fixed trait: whether one attacks and rebukes him or leaves him alone, he does not desist. Taḥmil here means an attack, not imposing a burden. Denial of God’s signs has become a deeply rooted vice, so that confronting further signs only increases their denial. Qaṣaṣ may mean either narrating by way of narration or recounting this particular account; its purpose is that people submit to truth and refrain from falsehood.

On verse (7:177), Al-Mizan says the verse both rebukes deniers and makes clear that they do not harm God: they alone suffer the consequences of their denial and therefore wrong themselves.

On verse (7:178), the commentary maintains that guidance bears its fruit only when accompanied by God’s guidance; other means do not constitute a complete cause of felicity. Likewise, error becomes a final loss only when God leads a person astray. Apparent īmān and taqwá do not by themselves save, nor do mere means of error by themselves damn; both guidance and misguidance depend on God’s will. Hence genuine, fruitful guidance is what God wills, while unguided appearances of guidance lack its reality, and the same applies to error. The definite articles in al-muhtadī and al-khāsirūn may indicate the perfection of guidance and loss rather than exclusivity; alternatively, they restrict real guidance and misguidance to God’s act, while God leads astray only transgressors.

Regarding verse (7:179), dharʾ means creation. The statement that many jinn and humans were created for hell does not conflict with the statement that creation is for mercy and paradise. Every action has a purpose as its perfection and another purpose in the end to which it necessarily leads. As not every piece of material can receive the form intended by a craftsman, some is necessarily discarded; this is a secondary, subordinate purpose by necessity (qaṣd ḍarūrī), arising from its lack of capacity for the intended perfection.

God created human beings to serve Him and enter His mercy, but the opposing causes of worldly life produce differing aptitudes, and not all acquire qualities suited to human perfection and felicity. His primary purpose is therefore mercy and paradise; His subordinate purpose by necessity is hell for the wretched who have lost their potential, even though they were created for paradise. The decree of felicity or damnation belongs to this latter purpose, which concerns God’s knowledge of each person’s ultimate end and is dictated by His subordinate, not His primary, will. Creating many jinn and humans for hell refers to this subordinate will.

Their hearts, eyes, and ears fail them because they do not place themselves where divine mercy and assistance reach them. They gain no benefit from the signs they see, the exhortations of those who follow truth, or the proofs inherent in fiṭrah. These faculties do not naturally cease to perform their created functions. Rather, God does not remove a blessing until people first alter what is in themselves. When they distort the path of serving Him, He punishes them by cancelling their potential, sealing their hearts, veiling their eyes, and deafening their ears; their incapacity to understand, see, and hear is an effect and sign of their course toward hell.

They resemble cattle because they forfeit the human capacity to distinguish good from evil and what benefits or harms human perfection through reason, sight, and hearing. Cattle particularly represent the elementary animal concerns of eating and mating, though animals also employ repelling powers to secure growth and procreation. Their straying is only relative: animals are guided to their own appointed ends through the faculties given to them, are not subject to human perfection, and are not blameworthy. These humans, however, possess the means and directions needed for perfection, yet neglect and disarrange them, using heart, sight, and hearing merely for animal pleasures. Their ḍalāl is consequently greater, and the blame truly belongs to them. Their heedlessness is not exclusive to them, but is found in them in its fullest reality; it results from God’s sealing of their faculties, and ghaflah is the root of all error and falsehood.
verses.180: Al-Mizan states that the most excellent names belong to Allah: supplicate Him by them, abandon those who profane them, and they will be requited for their deeds.
verses.181: Among God’s creatures is a community that guides by truth and does justice through it.
verses.182: Al-Mizan states: Those who deny God’s signs will be drawn imperceptibly into ruin without knowing it.
verses.183: God grants them respite, for His devising is sure.
verses.184: Al-Mizan states: Their companion has no madness; he is only a manifest warner.
verses.185: Al-Mizan asks why they do not contemplate the kingdom of the heavens and earth, all that Allah created, and the possible nearness of their end; after this, what discourse could they believe?
verses.186:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses distinguish guidance from error by one’s treatment of God’s excellent names. Human fiṭrah recognizes that the visible world depends on a reality that sustains and orders it: God, from Whom all things originate, to Whom they return, and from Whom every beauty and perfection comes. Those guided by God call upon and worship Him through names that affirm every perfection and exclude every defect. Those who commit sacrilege in His names either transfer His exclusive qualities to nature, idols, prophets, saints, or supposedly independent worldly causes, or ascribe to Him creaturely qualities and defects—physicality, location, sensory perception, temporal duration, human-like knowledge, will, and power, or unjust and ignorant action. Though these errors vary in degree, they are forms of straying whose path ends in hell.

Guidance is a positive reality belonging to God, whereas ḍalāl is the privation of His guidance and thus is not, in itself, an existent quality attributable to Him. When the Qur’an attributes misguidance to God, it means deprivation from His blessing as punishment for choosing error and rejecting His signs. This punishment works through imlāʾ, reprieve, and istidrāj, a step-by-step leading into temptation and ruin.

On (7:180), the commentary says that ism denotes either a word indicating a meaning or a proper name indicating a being. Because al-ḥusná means the highest goodness, beauty, or excellence, the names in the verse are descriptive names, not merely proper nouns. An excellent divine name denotes perfection and is free from every defect and non-existential aspect, unless that aspect can be abstracted away. Terms inseparable from material limitation, such as body, color, and size, cannot apply to God. But concepts such as knowledge, power, and life may be stripped of their human conditions: knowledge becomes encompassing a thing through its presence before the knower; power, giving existence; and life, possessing knowledge and power. Thus God has the realities of these perfections in a manner befitting His sanctity, not in the limited human manner.

The word order and the universal plural in the verse establish that every excellent name belongs to God alone in its reality. Others possess knowledge, life, creation, mercy, and the like only insofar as He bestows them, without diminishing His possession. The commentary rejects the claim that the article in al-asmāʾ restricts the verse to a known, enumerated set of names; the verses give no evidence for that reading.

Daʿwah can mean naming, calling, or worshipping. Although exegetes have proposed all three, Al-Mizan prefers worship: to supplicate God by His names is to worship and turn to Him while acknowledging the perfections they signify. Qur’anic usage equates calling with worship, and the verse’s promise that the profaners will be repaid for their actions supports this meaning, though naming and calling remain implications of worship. Yalḥadūna and yulḥidūna are synonymous readings, both meaning to incline away from the middle; their sacrilege is such a deviation in God’s names. Their requital answers the question naturally raised by the command to abandon them.

The nation of (7:181) is a real, divinely guided group among humankind. Genuine guidance comes only from God, cannot fail in its purpose, and protects from error; one who guides to truth is not guided by anyone other than God. Their guidance therefore indicates immunity from error through attachment to God. This may mean that the whole nation consists of prophets and saints, or that a whole group is described by a quality actually possessed by some of its members. In either case, their existence shows that such guidance is not beyond human capacity, for God has granted them His special guidance.

Istidrāj in (7:182) is gradual approach, here toward destruction in this world or the next. Its victims do not perceive their damnation because worldly glamour, pleasures, and occupations engross them. Al-Mizan considers two interpretations. On the accepted interpretation, their wrongdoing continually brings them nearer to ruin while God renews and prolongs their material bounties, so that they fail to reflect on their end. The alternative says that abandoning remembrance produces inward agitation, anxiety, and a constricted life; they then seek more worldly adornment, mistaking it for increased blessing while it deepens their punishment until eternal chastisement. Although this second sense accords with verses about rest in God’s remembrance and worldly wealth becoming punishment, it does not fit the following statement that God grants respite; the first interpretation must therefore be preferred.

Imlāʾ in (7:183) means postponement, delay, or extension. The shift from the preceding first-person plural to the singular may emphasize their deprivation from mercy and their being led to damnation. More particularly, the singular concerns postponement of judgment until its appointed time, a decree attributable to God alone; the plural in istidrāj suits the repeated renewal of blessings through angelic intermediaries. God’s sure devising explains both gradual ruin through blessings and the reprieve granted to its victims.

For (7:184), Al-Mizan takes the most direct construction to be two complete statements: the rhetorical, reproachful question, “Have they not reflected?” and the confirmation that there is no madness in their companion. Calling the Prophet their ṣāḥib directs them to his lifelong presence among them: had he been mad, they would have known it. What he brings is therefore a manifest warning, not madness. Jinnah may mean a particular kind of madness, or a jinn, reflecting the belief that a jinn could enter a person and speak through that person’s tongue.

Malakūt in (7:185) is the inner aspect of things by which they face and connect to their Lord; seeing this aspect is inseparable from yaqīn. The verse reproaches people for ignoring this divine dimension, which would disclose that the Prophet calls them to truth. They should consider the heavens, earth, and every created thing not merely as objects whose physical properties yield scientific knowledge, but as dependent beings connected to and directed by the Lord of the worlds. They should also consider that their death may already be near. Forgetfulness of death diverts people from their eternal life into worldly illusion, desires, and prolonged hopes; realizing that death may arrive at any time can uproot this heedlessness. “This” in the final question refers to the Qur’an, whose rational arguments, moral admonitions, and miraculous clarity leave no other discourse likely to make them believe.

Thus (7:186) explains why they will not believe: whomever Allah leads astray has no guide, and He leaves them bewildered in rebellion. ʿAmah may mean wandering in error or lack of understanding. The omitted counterpart, that no one can mislead whomever God guides, is unnecessary because the verse is answering why these people reject the Qur’an.

The commentary’s broader discussion begins from human awareness of need. People first know themselves, their faculties, and their dependence for survival; they then intuit a source that fulfills need and removes deficiency. The persistence of belief in some deity among even ancient and simple communities shows that belief in an origin of all things is demanded by fiṭrah, even when its application becomes distorted. Since all beings trace their existence to God, He possesses every perfection that He bestows—life, power, knowledge, hearing, sight, sustenance, mercy, and might—while He is free from the need and imperfection found in dependent things.

Negating imperfection often affirms its opposite: negating poverty affirms richness, weakness power, ignorance knowledge, and dishonor honor. Yet even a perfection found in creatures carries unsuitable conditions. Human knowledge, for example, depends on an external object, a mental image, senses, and organs; what belongs to God is its essential perfection, encompassing through presence, without these deficiencies. God must also be free from every limit, for a thing limited in its existence would require something greater to delimit it. His oneness therefore encompasses all beings without being encompassed.

From this freedom from limits Al-Mizan concludes that the divine attributes are identical with each other and with the divine essence in external reality, though conceptually distinct. If knowledge, power, or any attribute differed externally from the essence or from another attribute, each would limit the other; the divine essence would become composite and dependent on boundaries. This is incompatible with aḥadiyyah, which admits neither division nor external or mental multiplicity. The commentary rejects the purely apophatic claim that attributes such as knowledge, power, and life mean only freedom from their opposites, because it effectively denies all perfections affirmed by intuition and the Qur’an. It likewise rejects treating attributes as additions external to the essence, or affirming only their effects while negating the attributes themselves.

Divine attributes may be classified as thubūtiyyah, affirmative attributes of perfection, and salbiyyah, negational attributes expressing tanzīh, such as al-Quddūs and al-Subbūḥ. They are also attributes of essence, identical with the essence—life, power, and essential knowledge—or attributes of action, such as creation and sustenance, which are derived from divine acts and are additional to the essence. Attributes may further be nafsiyyah, independently meaningful and non-relational, like life; dhāt iḍāfah, independently meaningful but relational, like creation and fashioning; or iḍāfiyyah maḥḍah, purely relational, like creatorship and sustainership. Some names are used exclusively for God, such as Allāh and al-Raḥmān, though the meaning of mercy is found in creatures; the legal dimension of such usage lies beyond this exegetical discussion.

There is no real distinction between ṣifah and ism except what each primarily presents. An attribute first presents a quality in an essence, while a name first presents the essence viewed as qualified; thus “life” and “knowledge” are attributes, while “living” and “knowledgeable” are names. In either case, letters and sounds are only signs. The real divine names and attributes are the realities indicated, and the reality of God’s life is His very essence.

Creation receives its perfections through the divine attributes: God removes ignorance through His knowledge, impotence through His power, abasement through His glory, poverty through His richness, and sins through His forgiveness. In accordance with fiṭrah, one invokes the name relevant to one’s need: someone seeking wealth calls upon the Ever-Rich, Ever-Mighty, and Powerful, while someone seeking healing calls upon the Healer, Recoverer, Ever-Kind, and Ever-Merciful, not the Death-Giver or Vengeful. The Qur’an confirms this principle by ending its statements with names suited to their contents and using those names to establish its claims. Signs of beauty and majesty lead to the corresponding names, and those names lead to the divine essence on which all existence depends.

The names differ in scope just as their effects do. Hearing, sight, imagination, and intellection fall under knowledge; knowledge, power, life, and related qualities fall under sustenance, bestowal, blessing, and benevolence; these, together with pardon and forgiveness, fall under universal mercy. Divine life is broader than knowledge, which is broader than hearing, seeing, witnessing, subtlety, and awareness; similarly, the All-Merciful is broader than the Sustainer, which is broader than the Healer, Helper, and Guide. The names form a vertical order from restricted names with nothing beneath them to increasingly comprehensive names, culminating in the Greatest Name, al-ism al-aʿẓam, which embraces the realities of all names. The broader the name, the greater and more inclusive its effects; all effects and affairs ultimately return to the Greatest Name.

Al-Mizan rejects the popular conception of the Greatest Name as a hidden verbal formula whose letters, once discovered, would make all things subject to one’s will. Reports that may appear to support a letter-based understanding say that bism Allāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is nearer to the Greatest Name than the white of the eye to its black; that it is found in (2:255) and at the beginning of Āl-i ʿImrān; that its letters are dispersed in al-Ḥamd and can be assembled by the Imams; that Āṣaf ibn Barkhiyā summoned the Queen of Sheba’s throne through letters he knew; and that it consists of seventy-three letters, seventy-two given to prophets and one reserved in God’s hidden knowledge.

But causality shows that what acts in the universe is the existence of a thing, that a cause’s power corresponds to its degree of existence, and that cause and effect require a real existential correspondence. Uttered letters and sounds are accidental qualities, while their meanings are mental images; neither can independently wield external causal power, much less govern all things. God alone is the true cause. A divine name acts through its reality—God Himself viewed through the attribute proper to that name—not through its letters or conceived meaning.

God’s promise to answer prayer requires that the prayer be genuine and be directed to God alone. Whoever cuts off reliance on apparent means and turns wholly to God thereby connects to the reality of the name relevant to the request. The breadth of that name determines the breadth of the response; connection to the Greatest Name yields unconditional fulfillment because all things are subject to its reality. Reports that God taught a prophet or servant one of His names should therefore mean that He enabled complete detachment from all else and wholehearted turning to Him. Any spoken formula or mental conception is only a shell or instrument preserving that existential reality, not the Greatest Name itself.

The Qur’an does not limit God’s excellent names to a fixed number: every name that is excellent in meaning belongs to Him. Al-Mizan lists roughly 127 Qur’anic names, ranging from al-Abqá and al-ʿAfuww to al-Wāsiʿ and al-Ẓāhir, while maintaining that the names cannot be exhaustively numbered. Translator’s notes materially qualify this list: it omits names such as al-Faʿʿāl and Khayr al-nāṣirīn, perhaps Allāh; inconsistently includes annexed phrases; questionably counts al-Wālī and some adjectives as independent names; and does not consistently include names occurring in plural or comparable noun forms. These qualifications reinforce the commentary’s conclusion that every beautiful, perfect name belongs to God.

God is the sole real owner of these qualities. When creatures possess them, their possession is secondary, bestowed by Him, and never removes anything from His absolute ownership. Comparative and superlative names likewise indicate a common ground of meaning between God and creatures, while God possesses the reality primarily and perfectly.

Finally, Al-Mizan finds no exegetical evidence for tawqifiyyat al-asmāʾ, the restriction of divine names to transmitted scriptural wording. The argument drawn from (7:180) assumes both that the article in al-asmāʾ identifies a closed, previously known set and that sacrilege means using a non-transmitted name; both assumptions are disputable. Numerous reports saying that God has ninety-nine names and that whoever enumerates them enters paradise also do not establish such restriction. Exegetically, permissible descriptions exceed transmitted names. Jurisprudentially, however, caution requires avoiding formal appellation of God by names not found in the sources, while general permissible description remains broader.
verses.187: Al-Mizan presents the verse as directing the Prophet to answer that knowledge of the Hour belongs only to his Lord: Allah alone will manifest it at its time. It is heavy in the heavens and the earth and will come suddenly. Although people ask as though the Prophet were informed about it, most do not know.
verses.188:
Al-Mizan explains that the Hour is the time of humanity’s resurrection and return to God for His universal judgment. Although al-sāʿah has the definite article, the Qur’an and hadith use it as a proper name. In the question concerning its mursāhā, the intended sense is not a place or merely a time, but its occurrence and establishment: when will the Hour come to pass?

God’s sole manifestation of the Hour at its time means that its manifestation and its knowledge are inseparable. The Hour is a reality preserved in God’s unseen treasury, which He discloses when He wills. No other being can encompass it, because its occurrence entails the annihilation of everything other than God; no being can behold its own disappearance. Moreover, human knowledge depends on the causes and forces of this worldly system, whereas the Hour ends and transforms that entire system.

The commentary therefore holds that the Hour is heavy in every respect—its occurrence, knowledge, and features—not merely in one of the several senses proposed by exegetes. The heavens and earth cannot bear its manifestation because it entails their annihilation, and nothing can endure its own annihilation. God knows best. For the same reason it comes suddenly: none of its parts or features is known before its complete appearance, so it is abrupt and unanticipated for all beings.

The repeated question, phrased as though the Prophet were well-informed, indicates insistence. The polytheists apparently took his first answer, which referred knowledge to “my Lord,” as a courteous evasion by a servant rather than a direct acknowledgment of ignorance; they also took the statement that God alone manifests the Hour as describing its immensity without answering whether its time was known. They thus pressed him for a direct answer or an admission of ignorance. The final answer, “Its knowledge is only with Allah,” is instead a decisive statement made from knowledge: knowing that the Hour is known only to God is itself knowledge, not ignorance or mere deferment to one’s Lord. The change to “Allah” makes this clear.

Most people err because, accustomed to sensory knowledge, they suppose that every reality is knowable in the same way and that what they do not know is merely concealed from them. The verse rejects this assumption: unseen realities such as the Hour cannot be known by anyone but God, and their knowledge and reality are too heavy for any other being to bear.

Regarding (7:188), Al-Mizan states that the polytheists’ question wrongly assumed that claiming prophethood entails claiming knowledge of the unseen. God alone has genuine, independent knowledge of it; others know only through His revelation and teaching. Every being other than God is existentially limited and cannot access what lies beyond its limits, whereas God is unlimited and encompasses all things.

Rather than present this advanced reason to the Prophet’s audience, the verse gives an intelligible sign: knowledge of the unseen would disclose every benefit and harm, and one who possessed it would secure benefit and avoid harm. Thus the Prophet’s lack of control over benefit and harm, and the fact that he would otherwise have gained much good and suffered no ill, negate such knowledge from him. His true position is solely that of a messenger: a warner and bearer of good news to people who have faith.
verses.189: Al-Mizan states that God created humankind from a single soul and made its mate from it, so that the man might find comfort in her. After intercourse, she carries first a light burden and then, when pregnancy becomes heavy, the couple invoke their Lord and pledge gratitude if He grants them a healthy child.
verses.190: Al-Mizan says that, once given a healthy child, they ascribed partners to Allah concerning His gift, though He is exalted above their association.
verses.191: Al-Mizan asks how partners that are themselves created, create nothing, and can help neither their worshippers nor themselves can be ascribed to Allah.
verses.192: Al-Mizan asks how partners that are themselves created, create nothing, and can help neither their worshippers nor themselves can be ascribed to Allah.
verses.193: Al-Mizan states that calling these beings to guidance is futile: it makes no difference whether they are called or left unaddressed.
verses.194: Al-Mizan says those invoked besides Allah are servants like their invokers; if true, they should answer when called.
verses.195: Al-Mizan asks whether the alleged partners have feet to walk, hands to grasp, eyes to see, or ears to hear. The Prophet is commanded to challenge the polytheists to summon their partners and plot against him without delay.
verses.196: Allah, who sent down the Book, is the guardian and cares for the righteous.
verses.197: Those invoked besides Him help neither their invokers nor themselves.
verses.198:
Al-Mizan reads the verses as illustrating, in the experience of all the Children of Adam, humanity’s repeated breach of its covenant with God and its injustice toward His signs. “A single soul” is the father of each person, and the mate is from his own species, the woman in whom he finds comfort. taghashshāhā alludes to intercourse. The initially light burden is the zygote; as it develops, it becomes the heavy fetus. At that point the parents turn to God and, in effect, covenant with Him: if granted a healthy child, they will acknowledge the blessing as His alone, without attributing it to other causes or seeking refuge in anything besides Him.

The commentary explains that ṣāliḥan, literally “righteous,” here means sound in creation: a child fit to live, grow, and reach full human maturity without defect or deformity. Such a child is God’s rizq (provision, sustenance). Yet after receiving the child, parents commonly fall into shirk concerning this gift. Their love and concern lead them to cling to every available means, force, and safeguard for the child’s protection and upbringing, thereby breaking their pledge to thank God alone. This is the condition of most people, except those granted God’s special mercy. Parents may not consciously formulate the prayer or make it ritually, but when cut off from all means in anxiety over a child, their hearts sincerely turn to God, like those overwhelmed by waves at sea; once safety is granted, they return to dependence on other means.

The plural yushrikūna, rather than a dual form, confirms that the account concerns humankind generally rather than a particular pair such as Adam and Eve. Had the passage concerned only that pair, its ending should have used the dual. Moreover, the following verses condemn shirk in the evident sense of serving another god, which cannot be attributed to Adam. Adam was chosen and guided by God, and one whom God guides does not go astray; service of other than God is among the gravest forms of error and straying.

Al-Mizan considers and rejects several alternatives. One view takes the shirk to be only subtle reliance on apparent means, a failure to preserve the complete khulūṣ (purity, sincerity) implied by gratitude. On this account, the grateful are the chosen servants of God, beyond Satan’s access, and Adam and Eve merely fell short of perfect dedication while arranging their child’s care. The commentary replies that the plural wording remains unexplained, and that the shirk in the following verses plainly means serving other gods, not mere inward distraction by natural means. Another view makes only the opening statement about Adam and Eve, then shifts to all people, analogizing this to a verse that moves from a universal address to those sailing in ships. Al-Mizan finds no equally decisive contextual indicator of such a shift here, which would be contrary to Qur’anic eloquence, unless the plural conclusion and following verses are made the evidence. It therefore regards this as a mixture of its own interpretation and the preceding view. A third proposal supplies an omitted phrase, making Adam and Eve’s children, rather than Adam and Eve themselves, the associators; the commentary finds no evidence for it. Finally, reports that Adam and his wife committed shirk are dismissed as fabricated or distorted because they contradict the Qur’an.

For (7:191-193), Al-Mizan holds that the first challenge may concern either physical idols or any means or force relied upon apart from God, since such reliance is shirk. The following verses, however, apparently concern physical idols specifically: they cannot aid their worshippers or themselves and do not know whether they are called. Verse (7:194-195) explains this judgment. Those invoked besides God are servants, created and directed by God just as their worshippers are. The demand that they answer their invokers refutes the polytheists’ implied claim that their gods possess knowledge and power. Their depicted feet, hands, eyes, and ears are only carved or painted shapes; the idols are inanimate. The use of ʿibād (servants) thus includes physical objects.

The command to the Prophet to summon the partners and let them plot against him continues his argument against the polytheists. Their inability to act shows the difference between their path and his: the Lord of Muḥammad alone possesses all knowledge and power, whereas their gods have neither the knowledge to reach anything nor the power to support their worshippers. The Prophet is to declare that Allah, who sent down the Book for guidance, is his guardian, cares for His righteous servants, and will therefore assist him and repel their plot. The idols can aid neither others nor themselves; they neither hear nor see, and have neither knowledge nor power. The command also implies that the Prophet belongs to al-ṣāliḥīn (the righteous), a title which the commentary says the Qur’an has not affirmed for any other prophet. Like earlier prophets before their peoples, he challenges both the idols and those who worship them.
verses.199: Forgive, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.
verses.200: Al-Mizan states: If Satan tempts you, seek Allah’s protection; He is All-Hearing and All-Knowing.
verses.201: Al-Mizan states: When Satan touches the Godwary, they remember Allah and perceive.
verses.202: Their brethren draw them into error and do not stop.
verses.203: Al-Mizan states: When asked for a verse, say: I follow only my Lord’s revelation, which is insight, guidance, and mercy for believers.
verses.204: Al-Mizan states: When the Qur’ān is recited, listen silently, that you may receive mercy.
verses.205: Al-Mizan states: Remember your Lord inwardly, beseechingly and reverentially, quietly morning and evening; do not be heedless.
verses.206:
Al-Mizan presents these closing verses as returning to the chapter’s central purpose: they direct the Prophet to a beautiful conduct that attracts hearts and gives souls peace, then to tadhakkur and finally dhikr.

“Cling” (akhdh) means to hold fast. On the common reading, clinging to ʿafw means persistently overlooking wrongs done to oneself and foregoing personal retaliation. It does not authorize forgiving violations of others’ rights: that would encourage mischief, further injure people, and violate the laws preserving society, contrary to the Qur’anic prohibitions of injustice, corruption, and supporting oppressors. The Prophet accordingly overlooked personal offences; however, reports from Imam al-Ṣādiq interpret ʿafw as wasaṭ, a balanced middle course. Al-Mizan considers this interpretation more fitting and inclusive, since taking ʿafw merely as pardon risks making the command to turn away from the ignorant repetitive.

Al-ʿurf and maʿrūf denote practices rational people recognize as good, unlike munkar, what collective reason repudiates. Enjoining al-ʿurf therefore means enjoining every good deed, while the one who enjoins it must observe it and must enjoin it in a good rather than objectionable manner. Turning away from ignorant or foolish people means meeting them with tolerance and moderation, the most effective means of neutralizing their folly and escaping its harm; responding foolishly only confirms and prolongs their error.

Nazgh can mean destructive interference, provocation to an unhealthy response, or Satan’s slightest temptation. In this context it especially means Satan’s attempt to provoke anger through the ignorant person’s behavior and to induce an equally foolish response. Although addressed to the Prophet, the command is intended for his community, since he is immune to Satanic insinuation: when so disturbed, they should seek God’s protection, for He hears and knows.

A ṭāʾif min al-shayṭān may mean either a devil circling the heart to plant evil or an evil temptation circling it to enter; both amount to the same thing. Tadhakkur is reflection that leads to a conclusion previously overlooked or unknown. When the Godwary are touched by Satan, they remember that God is their Lord, that they belong to Him, that He cares for them, and that all their affairs are in His hand. By entrusting those affairs to Him, they are spared Satan’s burden and plot, the veil of heedlessness is removed, and they perceive. The comparison with “Indeed he [Satan] does not have any authority over those who have faith and put their trust in their Lord” (16:99) shows that istiʿādhah is both tawakkul and tadhakkur: it realizes that God alone is refuge against Satan despite his power.

In contrast, “their brethren” in verse (7:202) are the devils, the brethren of the polytheists. The verse apparently describes their condition: devils continually draw the polytheists into error and do not desist, or the polytheists themselves do not stop or withdraw from that error.

The polytheists’ demand for a verse is mockery. They deny the verses brought to them, but when revelation is delayed they ask why the Prophet does not selectively assemble one of the alleged divine signs himself. The reply establishes that revelation is not his choice: he follows only what his Lord reveals. “This” is the Qur’an, through which God gives insight; it is guidance and mercy for those who have faith.

To listen and be silent when the Qur’ān is recited means to give it attentive hearing in silence. The command is general, even though some hold that it was revealed particularly concerning recitation in congregational prayer.

Verse (7:205) enjoins two forms of dhikr: inward remembrance in the heart and subdued verbal remembrance. Loud dhikr is not excluded because it is not dhikr, but because it conflicts with the etiquette of servitude. Al-Mizan cites a Prophetic report in which, when Companions shouted Allāhu akbār during an expedition, the Prophet told them that the One they called was neither far nor absent. Taḍarruʿ is humble entreaty that inclines toward and seeks nearness to God, while khīfah is an awe that holds one back before His sacred presence. Together they produce an orientation both toward God through love and away through awe.

God is pure good, and evil reaching human beings arises from their own deficiency. As Dhū al-jalāl wa al-ikrām, He has names of beauty that attract all things and names of majesty that dominate and repel them. Proper remembrance encompasses both, and thus combines hope with fear, beseeching with reverence. “Morning and evening” apparently qualifies the subdued verbal dhikr and corresponds to some obligatory daily prayers; a translator’s note adds that it may instead mean continual remembrance, applying to inward and verbal dhikr alike. The prohibition is not against every passing lapse, but against becoming one of those deeply marked by heedlessness. One must not let it settle in the heart, but recover remembrance immediately whenever one becomes heedless. The verse therefore commands constant inward remembrance with entreaty and awe, and quiet verbal remembrance morning and evening.

Verse (7:206) justifies this command: one should remember God in this manner in order to be among those near Him. Those “with your Lord” are not confined to angels, as most exegetes say, but include whoever is near God; ʿinda Rabbika implies presence rather than absence. Nearness to God corresponds to one’s remembrance of Him, for mindfulness removes the veil between servant and Lord. Apart from this veil, all beings stand in an equal relation to God, without real difference of nearness or distance.

Not disdaining worship, glorifying God, and prostrating may describe inward states as well as spoken remembrance and bodily acts: the heart can be free of pride, glorify God, and be utterly humble in prostration. Tasbīḥ and sujūd need not be performed only by tongue and limbs, as the Qur’an attributes praise and prostration to all things. These three requirements are lighter than the uninterrupted worship described in (21:19-20) and (41:38). Those verses concern continual glorification without pause or other engagement, whereas the present verses require the lower stage of preventing heedlessness from becoming established in the heart. God is the Knower.
